en: The Mirror of Composition by Śrī [Viśvanātha], Containing Only the Verses (1)
May that Goddess of Speech, whose splendor is as beautiful as the autumnal moon, first illuminate my mind;
having dispelled the perpetual darkness, may she reveal all meanings. (VisSd 1.1)

Since the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life occurs through poetry alone, even for those of limited intellect by means of its aesthetic pleasure, its essential nature is therefore defined here.

Poetry consists of aesthetic flavor (rasa); its defects are those which cause its diminution, while its excellences (guṇas), ornaments (alaṅkāras), and stylistic modes (rītis) are declared to be the causes of its enhancement.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Definition of the Nature of Poetry," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa. (2) Second Light.
A sentence (vākya) is a collection of words endowed with semantic competency (yogyatā), expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), and proximity (satti).
A collection of sentences is a great sentence (mahā-vākya); thus, a sentence is considered to be of two kinds. 2.1.
Phonemes (varṇa) are those capable of being employed in linguistic usage that convey a single integrated meaning;
the meaning (artha) is considered to be threefold: the expressed (vācya), the indicated (lakṣya), and the suggested (vyaṅgya). 2.2.

The denoted meaning is understood through denotation (*abhidhā*); the indicated meaning is considered understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and the suggested meaning is understood through suggestion (*vyañjanā*). These are the three powers of a word. (ViśSd 2.3)
In that regard, the former [type of word] is considered [to function] by conveying a conventional meaning;
the convention is grasped with respect to a genus, as well as qualities, substances, and actions. (VisSd 2.4)

When the primary meaning is sublated, that power by which another meaning connected to it is understood—whether through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*)—is designated as *lakṣaṇā*. (VisSd 2.5)

When the primary meaning implies another for the sake of establishing its connection within the sentence-meaning—even by including itself—this is "indication based on inclusion" (upādāna-lakṣaṇā). VisSd 2.6.

The surrendering of one's own [primary] meaning for the sake of establishing the connection of another is the definition of *lakṣaṇā* based on indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), because it serves as the cause [for that connection]. (VisSd 2.7)
Each of these [two types] is further divided into two by means of superimposition (*āropa*) and identification (*adhyavasāna*).
They bring about the cognition of the identity of another in a subject that is not swallowed up [by it]. (VisSa 2.8)
That [metaphor] in which [the object] is swallowed is considered *sādhyavasānikā* (of the nature of identification).
All of these, whether based on similarity or other relations, are pure (*śuddha*).
However, because it is based on similarity, the secondary (gauṇī) function is considered to have sixteen varieties;
the indicative (lakṣaṇā) function, which results in a fruit, is of two kinds according to whether the suggested meaning is hidden or unhidden. (VisSd 2.10)
Since they pertain to both the substratum (dharmin) and the attributes (dharma), these [perfections] are also twofold with respect to their fruit.
Thus, the wise consider that there are forty varieties of characteristics due to this lack of distinction.

Each of those [functions] is also twofold, according as they reside in words or in sentences; when the primary functions such as denotation (abhidhā) have ceased, another meaning is understood. (VisSd 2.12)
That function is called *vyañjanā* (suggestion), belonging to both word and meaning;
based on *abhidhā* (denotation) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the *vyañjanā* of a word is twofold.

When a word with multiple meanings is restricted to a single meaning by means of context such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, that which causes the cognition of another [unrestricted] meaning is *vyañjanā* (suggestion), which relies upon *abhidhā* (denotation). (VisSd 2.14)
That for whose sake a thing possessing a characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is perceived is the purpose (prayojana);
that by which [the purpose] is rejected would be indication (vyañjanā), based upon indication (lakṣaṇā). (VisSd 2.15)

Of the speaker, the person to be addressed, and the sentence; of other proximate factors and the expressed meaning; of the context, place, and time; and of tone, gestures, and so forth— [these are the causes of ambiguity]. (ViSd 2.16)
That which makes known another object by virtue of its specific distinction is "possessing an object" (sārtha-sambhavā).
Because objects are of three kinds, this [non-perception] is considered to be of three types for each of those three. (VisSd 2.17)
The meaning, which is to be understood through the word, manifests [itself]; the word, moreover, relies upon other meanings.
When one [factor] acts as a manifestor, the other serves as its cooperative cause.
Due to its association with the three limiting adjuncts—denotation and the others—the word is also considered to be of three kinds:
denotative, indicative, and likewise suggestive.
Others say that there is a function called *tātparya* (implicature) for the purpose of bringing about the cognition of the connection between word-meanings;
they hold that this is the *tātparyārtha* (the intended meaning), and that the sentence is the means of cognizing it.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Nature of the Sentence," in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
(3) The Third Chapter.

Through the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and likewise the transitory states (*saṃcārin*), the stable emotion (*sthāyībhāva*) such as love attains the state of *rasa* for those possessed of consciousness. (VisSd 3.1)
Through the predominance of *sattva*, it consists of consciousness whose nature is the bliss of light and sound that is indivisible;
it is devoid of contact with any other object of knowledge and is like a twin brother to the savoring of Brahman.
This aesthetic flavor (rasa), whose very life is the transcendental wonder, is relished by certain subjects as non-different from their own mental forms. 3.3.

Even in aesthetic sentiments such as compassion, that supreme bliss which arises is attested solely by the experience of those possessed of sensitivity; this is the only authority in that regard. (VisSd 3.4)
Furthermore, when there is suffering in those [stories], no one would be intent upon them;
likewise, works such as the Rāmāyaṇa would become causes of suffering.
Since the causality of grief, joy, and so forth arises from worldly conventions, let worldly grief, joy, and the like indeed arise in the world. (VisSd 3.6)
What harm is there in the fact that, for those who have attained the state of transcending worldly mental fluctuations through recourse to poetry, happiness arises from all of them? VisSd 3.7.
Similarly, the shedding of tears and so forth are considered to arise from the rapidity of the mind;
that savoring [of the emotion] does not occur without the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and the like.
The function of the excitants (vibhāva) and the other factors is the universalization [of them] by name;
through their power, [the hero's] acts such as leaping across the ocean and so forth became possible. (VisSd 3.9)
The cognizer realizes his own self as non-different from that [object];
the perception of its destruction and so forth arises from the conceit of commonality.
Even for human beings, there is no fault in leaping across the ocean and so forth;
likewise, aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like are perceived through their commonality. (VisSd 3.11)
Regarding another as "not another," and regarding "mine" as "not mine"—in the relishing of that state, no discernment of its fading away and so forth exists. (VisSd 3.12)
For those who have attained the supramundane activity of meditative cultivation and so forth, this very supramundane nature is an ornament, not a defect. (VisSd 3.13)

For even though, according to worldly convention, the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors function as causes, effects, and transitory states, they are considered to be exclusively causes for the arousal of rasa. 3.14.
First, each [element] as it is being perceived is called a cause;
thereafter, all of them—vibhāva and the rest—combined together [constitute the cause] for those possessed of consciousness.

If the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) were to exist as something to be relished through the analogy of the taste of a refreshing drink (*prapāṇaka*), it would have to reside either in all three factors—the excitants (*vibhāva*), etc.—together, or in one or the other of them. (3.16)
At that time, when another [object] is suddenly projected, no fault exists,
because of its limitation, its worldly nature, and likewise its being subject to interruption.
The awakening of the emotion (rati) and so forth belonging to the character being portrayed would not constitute rasa;
for [the emotion] would merely consist of the actual nature of Rāghava and others through the mere practice of training and so forth. (VisSd 3.18)
Just as a dancer who displays [a performance] does not himself become a relisher of the aesthetic flavor (rasa),
so too this spectator, through his engagement with the meaning of the poetry, becomes a worthy recipient of the term "connoisseur" (sabhya).
This [cognition] is not something to be made known regarding its own existence, because it is invariably perceived;
for it consists of a collective mental apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the various aspects such as cessation and so forth.
Therefore, it is neither an effect nor eternal, being devoid of prior cognition;
for at the time when there is no cognition, its very existence is not found.
Nor will it be future, because its nature is self-luminous and consists of bliss; nor is it present, because its existence is distinct from both effects and objects of cognition.
Because it is the object of the reflective awareness of the dispassionate and others, and because it is clearly experienced by the wise as consisting of supreme bliss. (VisSd 3.23)
Non-conceptual cognition is not accepted as its apprehender, because it lacks the capacity for association with verbal expression. (VisSd 3.24)
It is cognizable through conceptual construction, yet it is not a direct perception;
its manifestation is not indirect, because it arises from verbal testimony. (VisSd 3.25)
Therefore, this extraordinary reality must truly be known by those with aesthetic sensitivity;
for the wise maintain that in this case, the means of knowledge is nothing other than the act of relishing itself.
The accomplishment of this savoring [of the aesthetic flavor] through its own perfection is used figuratively;
I shall explain its inexpressibility and other qualities in the context of defining its nature as suggestion (*vyañjanā*). (3.27)
Since rasa arises precisely from its identity with the cognition of love (*rati*) and so forth, its self-luminosity and indivisibility are thereby established. (VisSd 3.28)

In the world, the excitants (*vibhāvas*) are the factors that awaken passion and the like; in poetry and drama, two types of them are traditionally recognized, known as the objective (*ālambana*) and the evocative (*uddīpana*).
The objective is the hero and so forth, for it is by taking him as the support that the emergence of rasa occurs. (VisSd 3.29)

A leader is one who is generous, accomplished, of noble birth, possessed of great fortune, endowed with beauty, youth, and energy, skillful, beloved by the people, and characterized by brilliance, cleverness, and virtuous conduct. (VisSd 3.30)
The *dhīrodātta*, the *dhīroddhata*, as well as the *dhīralalita* and the *dhīrapraśānta*: thus has this first [type] been described as having four divisions.
One who is free from boastfulness, patient, exceedingly profound, and of great being;
steadfast, with hidden pride, firm in his vows—he is described as the "dignified and noble" (dhīrodātta). VisSd 3.32.
One who is devoted to illusion, fierce, fickle, and full of egoism and pride; one who is intent on self-praise—such a person is described by the wise as "the haughty hero" (dhīroddhata). VisSd 3.33.
Free from anxiety, gentle, constantly devoted to the arts, and firm-yet-graceful, he should be;
possessing abundant common virtues, he should be a "firm-and-peaceful" type, such as the divine and so forth. (VisSd 3.34)
By these sixteen types—namely, the *dakṣiṇa*, *dhṛṣṭa*, *anukūla*, and *śaṭha*—[the hero is classified].
Among these, the one who feels equal passion toward many women is called *dakṣiṇa*. (VisSd 3.35)
Though he has committed offenses, he is fearless; though rebuked, he is not ashamed;
though his faults have been seen, he speaks falsely—such is the audacious leader.
This deceitful man is devoted to one woman while being favorable toward another;
though he displays outward affection for one, he secretly practices what is disagreeable toward the other. (VisSd 3.37)
And because these are of three kinds—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—it is said that there are forty-eight varieties of heroes. (VisSd 3.38)

However, in the incidental narrative (prāsaṅgika-itivṛtta) that extends far [beyond the main plot], his companion known as the *pīṭhamarda* should be slightly inferior to him in qualities. (VisSd 3.39)
The companions of this [hero] are the *viṭa*, the *ceṭa*, the *vidūṣaka*, and others;
they are devoted, skilled in jests, capable of breaking the pride of angry women, and pure. (Viśvāmitraśāstra 3.40)

But the *viṭa* is a rogue who lacks the excellence of enjoyment; he knows only a portion of the arts, is skilled in the courtesan’s arts, eloquent, sweet-tongued, and highly esteemed in social circles. (VisSd 3.41)

The Vidūṣaka shall be one whose name is Kusuma, Vasantaka, or the like; his body is that of a servant, and by means of dress, speech, and so forth, he causes laughter, delights in quarrels, and is skilled in his own duties.
Likewise, a minister should be employed for the deliberation of affairs and for matters concerning the harem;
these include dwarfs, eunuchs, Kirātas, Mlecchas, Ābhīras, Śakāras, hunchbacks, and the like.
Arrogant, foolish, and conceited, born of a low family yet endowed with power—this brother-in-law of the king, whose brother remains unmarried, is known as Śakāra. (VisSd 3.44)
In the case of punishment, there should be friends, princes, forest-dwellers, vassals, soldiers, and so forth;
likewise, in the case of dharma, there should be officiating priests, family chaplains, knowers of Brahman, and ascetics.
The *pīṭhamarda* and others are declared to be superior; the *viṭa* and *vidūṣaka* are middling;
likewise, the *śakāra*, *ceṭa*, and others are proclaimed to be inferior. (VisSd 3.46)
The messenger is of three kinds: one with full authority, one with limited authority, and likewise one who merely carries a message;
the servant sent on business is also of these three types, and female messengers are likewise of such kinds.

Having inferred the intentions of both parties, he himself provides the answer and carries out the task effectively; such a person is known as a *nisṛṣṭārtha* (an envoy with full discretionary powers).
One who speaks only what is measured is a speaker of measured meaning; one who accomplishes the task is a fulfiller of the purpose.
One who conveys the message exactly as it was spoken is a messenger. (VisSd 3.49)
Beauty, grace, sweetness, profundity, fortitude, splendor, charm, and magnanimity—these eight are the human qualities born of the quality of goodness (sattva). (VisSd 3.50)
Bravery, skill, truthfulness, great enthusiasm, and affection,
as well as rivalry toward those who are base or even superior— where these qualities exist, they know that to be "splendor" (śobhā).
A steady gaze, a varied gait, speech accompanied by a smile during playful gestures, and an absence of agitation even amidst disturbances—this is proclaimed as sweetness (*mādhurya*). (VisSd 3.52)
Gambhirya is the state of being changeless despite fear, grief, anger, joy, and the like;
dhairya is the lack of wavering from one's resolve even in the face of great obstacles. (VisSd 3.53)
The inability to endure insults, contempt, and the like, even when inflicted by another at the risk of one's life, is declared to be *tejas* (vitality). (VisSd 3.54)
Sweetness of speech and dress, as well as graceful amorous gestures, constitute *lalita* (grace).
Generosity accompanied by kind speech, and equanimity toward both enemy and friend, constitute *audārya* (magnanimity). (VisSd 3.55)
Now, the heroine is of three types: one's own, another's, and a common woman;
she is endowed with the general qualities of a hero as far as possible. (VisSd 3.56)

One's own wife, who is endowed with discipline, straightforwardness, and other virtues, devoted to household duties, and faithful to her husband, is also said to be of three types: the innocent (mugdhā), the intermediate (madhyā), and the bold (pragalbhā). (VisSd 3.57)
A young woman who has newly entered the transformations of youth and passion is called *vāmā* in sexual union;
she is gentle in her indignation and possesses excessive modesty—such a one is known as *mugdhā*. (VisSd 3.58)
The middle woman is characterized by diverse amorous play, possessing fully developed passion and youth;
she is considered to have somewhat bold speech and moderate shyness. (VisSd 3.59)
Blinded by passion, in the full bloom of youth, and skilled in all forms of lovemaking; elevated in emotion, with slight bashfulness, she overcomes her lover through her boldness. (VisSd 3.60)

They are both steadfast and unsteadfast; thus, among the six types [of heroines], the steadfast-middling heroine (madhyā-dhīrā) would burn with anger through a dear, yet sarcastic and indirect speech.
The steadfast-unsteady woman is recognized by her weeping; the unsteady woman, by her masculine speech;
and if the bold woman should be steadfast, she then conceals the outward form of her anger.
In that sexual union, the *dhīrādhīrā* remains indifferent while displaying outward respect; however, she distresses the man with sarcastic remarks. (VisSd 3.63)
One should threaten or strike others; each of those [women] is also of two kinds, according to whether they are junior or senior in relation to the lover's affection. (VisSd 3.64)
Therefore, twelve varieties of the *madhyā* and *pragalbhā* types are proclaimed;
since the *mugdhā* is only one, there are thirteen varieties of the *svīyā* (one's own) woman.

The woman belonging to another is said to be of two kinds: the married woman and the maiden; likewise, the married woman who has abandoned her husband for reasons such as a journey, and the unchaste woman whose modesty has vanished. (VisSd 3.66)
But a maiden who has not yet been married, possessing modesty and fresh youth, being self-possessed and skilled in the arts, is the common courtesan heroine. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.67)
She feels no aversion toward those devoid of virtues, nor does she feel attachment even toward those possessed of virtues;
having observed merely his wealth, she displays outward passion.
Even if she has accepted him, she may expel a man whose wealth is exhausted, out of a desire for a future reunion. (VisSd 3.69)
Thieves, eunuchs, fools, those who have obtained wealth easily, and those who merely wear the outward signs while concealing lust and other vices—these are generally her favorites. (VisSd 3.70)
She too, though devoted to truth, is under the sway of passion;
whether she is attached or detached, her devotion to truth lies in her sexual pleasure.
These eight states become sixteen when divided; likewise, there are the woman whose husband is under her control, the neglected wife, and the woman going to meet her lover. VisSd 3.72.
The woman separated by a quarrel, the deceived woman, the one whose husband is away, the woman prepared for a lover, and likewise the woman longing in separation. (VisSd 3.73)
She whose beloved, drawn by her qualities of passion, does not leave her side,
and who is intent on various amorous dalliances, is one who has her husband under her control.
She whose lover comes to her side marked with the signs of union with another is called "the betrayed" (khaṇḍitā) by the wise, being stained by the bitterness of jealousy.
She who, being under the sway of the god of love, causes her beloved to come to her, or goes to him herself, is called an *abhisārikā* by the wise. (VisSd 3.76)
If a woman of noble birth should approach him, she should remain withdrawn within her own limbs, keep her ornaments silent, and be veiled by a head-covering.
But if she should be pursued by courtesans, she should have a variegated and radiant dress, with tinkling anklets and bracelets, and a face smiling with joy.
If she should approach as a female messenger, her conversation would be faltering with intoxication, her eyes wide with amorous confusion, and her gait and movements languidly swaying.
A field, a garden, a ruined temple, the house of a messenger, a forest, a garland-maker’s shop, a cremation ground, and likewise the banks of rivers and so forth. (VisSd 3.80)
Thus, for the diversion of unchaste women who have arranged a rendezvous,
there are eight locations, as well as any place whatsoever concealed by darkness.
But she who, out of anger, casts aside even her lord of life who speaks to her with endearing words, and later experiences remorse, is one separated by a quarrel.
She who, even after making an appointment with her lover, does not come into his presence,
should be known as a deceived woman, utterly humiliated.
She whose husband has gone to a distant land due to various duties, and who is afflicted by the suffering born of love, is called a woman whose husband is away (proṣitabhartṛkā). (VisSd 3.84)
She who adorns herself when her chamber for the rendezvous has been prepared, having learned of the arrival of her beloved, is known as *vāsaka-sajjā*. (VisSd 3.85)
Even though her beloved has resolved to come, if he does not arrive due to fate,
she suffers from the pain of his non-arrival and is tormented by the longing of separation.
Thus, there are one hundred and twenty-eight varieties according to their superior, middling, and inferior natures;
these constitute three hundred and eighty-four distinct types of heroines.
In some instances, a mutual intermingling of these [defects] is observed in actual examples;
other innumerable defects also exist, but they have not been mentioned here for fear of prolixity.
Among those born of youth in their twenty-eight varieties, there are three types of ornaments arising from the body: *bhāva*, *hāva*, and *helā*. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.89)
Beauty, loveliness, brilliance, sweetness, eloquence, magnanimity,
and steadfastness— these seven alone are born without effort.

Playfulness (*līlā*), graceful movement (*vilāsa*), charm (*vicchitti*), affected indifference (*bibboka*), the mingling of emotions (*kilakiñcita*), affected bashfulness (*moṭṭāyita*), playful coquetry (*kuṭṭamita*), bewilderment (*vibhrama*), elegance (*lalita*), and intoxication (*mada*). (VisSd 3.91)
Sporting, heating, innocence, distraction, curiosity, laughter, alarm, and play—these are the eighteen [types of amorous gestures]. (VisSd 3.92)
Although the ten states, beginning with existence and intrinsic nature, occur for persons, existence is the first modification within the mind, which is by nature immutable. (VisSd 3.93)

But *bhāva* itself, which manifests the desire for enjoyment through transformations of the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth, when its transformations are only slightly perceptible, is called *hāva*. (VisSd 3.94)
That very [state] becomes a transformation characterized by extreme ease and equanimity;
it is the adornment of the limbs through beauty, youth, grace, enjoyment, and so forth. (VisSd 3.95)
That very luster, its radiance nourished by the god of love, is called *kānti*;
that same luster, when exceedingly expansive, is designated as *dīpti*.
In all particular states, there is sweetness, loveliness,
fearlessness, confidence, magnanimity, and constant discipline.
Self-praise from one who is liberated, steadfastness, and an unshakable state of mind—[these are not to be shown] through limbs, dress, ornaments, nor even by affectionate words. (VisSd 3.98)

They know *līlā* (playful imitation) to be the imitation of a beloved by means of those things motivated by affection—namely, the movements of walking, standing, sitting, and so forth, as well as the actions of the face, eyes, and other limbs. (VisSd 3.99)

*Vilāsa* (grace) is a particular kind of charm arising from the sight of a beloved and so forth; *vicchitti* (elegance) is even a slight arrangement of ornaments that serves to nourish beauty. (VisSd 3.100)
*Kilakiñcita* is the mingling of smiles, dry weeping, laughter, terror, anger, fatigue, and so forth, arising from the joy produced by union with a beloved woman and similar causes. (VisSd 3.101)
When the mind is permeated by the state of being that [beloved], scratching the ear and so forth during conversations and the like with the beloved is called *moṭṭāyita*. (VisSd 3.102)
When there is agitation due to joy even while grasping the hair, breasts, lips, and so forth,
they say that the shaking of the head and hands is called *kuṭṭamita*.
Vibhrama (confusion) is considered to be the misplaced application of gestures such as confusion due to haste, joy, passion, and so forth, on occasions such as the arrival of a beloved. (VisSd 3.104)

The graceful arrangement of limbs due to their delicateness constitutes *lalita* (grace). *Mada* (intoxication) is a transformation born from the pride of good fortune, youth, and so forth. (VisSd 3.105)
Even at the time for speaking, remaining silent out of shame is considered *vihṛtam*;
*tapana* consists of the behavior arising from the impulse of passion (*smaravega*) during separation from a beloved. (Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā 3.106)
That questioning of even a well-known object as if out of ignorance in the presence of a beloved is called "simplicity" by those who know its true nature. (VisSd 3.107)
Half-adornment of ornaments, looking about falsely, speaking of secrets, and slight distraction in the presence of the beloved. (Viṣṇu-saṃhitā 3.108)
Curiosity (*kutūhala*) is the longing that arises upon beholding a beautiful object;
whereas *hasita* is frivolous laughter born from the emergence of youth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.109)
In the presence of her beloved, being startled and filled with fear and agitation, while sporting together with her lover in a pleasure grove—this is called *kelī* (amorous play). VisSd 3.110.

Upon seeing [the beloved], she shows bashfulness; she does not look him directly in the face; or she sees her lover when he is hidden, or when he is wandering about, or when he has passed by. (VisSd 3.111)
Even when questioned in many ways, she generally speaks only a little of what is pleasing, with a very slow and soft voice, her face cast downwards and her speech faltering. (VisSd 3.112)
Constantly attentive to the stories concerning him when told by others,
the young woman, full of passion for her beloved, directs her gaze elsewhere while listening.
She highly prizes staying in the presence of her beloved for a long time;
yet, if she goes before him without being adorned, she does not even come within the path of his vision.
In some cases, under the pretext of binding her hair or adjusting her garment, she may clearly reveal the base of her arms, her breasts, or the lotus of her navel. *Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā* 3.115.
He provides clothing and other necessities for the attendants of his beloved;
he places trust in his friends and shows them great honor. (VisSd 3.116)
In the midst of her friends, she speaks of his virtues; she bestows her own wealth upon him;
she sleeps when he sleeps; and in his suffering, she bears his suffering, and in his happiness, his happiness. (VisSd 3.117)
Standing constantly within the range of his vision, she gazes at her beloved from afar; yet, as if overcome by the transformations of passion, she addresses her attendants directly in his presence.
Whatever she sees, she laughs pointlessly;
likewise, she scratches her ear, loosens her braid, and ties it up again. (VisSd 3.119)
She yawns, stretches her limbs, embraces and kisses the boy,
and likewise applies a tilaka mark upon the forehead of her female companion.
She draws with the tip of her big toe, gazes with a sidelong glance,
bites her own lower lip, and speaks sweet words while looking downward.
And the Leader does not leave that place where he is seen;
he comes to his house under some pretext of business. (VisSd 3.122)
She gazes repeatedly at whatever has been given by her beloved once it is placed upon her body;
she is constantly delighted in his company, but in his absence, she becomes dejected and emaciated.
She considers that conduct to be great, she considers what is dear to him to be dear;
she seeks things of little value, and when asleep, she does not turn over. VisSd 3.124.
A devoted, broad-hipped woman, facing him, does not experience any sattvic transformations; she speaks words that are pleasant, true, and affectionate. (VisSd 3.125)

In these [situations], the actions of a young woman are characterized by excessive modesty; those of a middle-aged woman by moderate shame; and those of an older woman by failing modesty. (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 3.126)
For another woman who is bold, as well as for a courtesan, [the advances] should be made through the sending of letters, affectionate glances, and gentle speech. (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 3.127)
The manifestation of a woman's inner state is sought through the dispatching of female messengers;
these messengers are a female friend, an actress, a maidservant, a nurse, or a neighbor. (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 3.128)
Young women, female renunciants, artisans, and craftsmen, as well as others [should be employed];
likewise, skill in the arts, enthusiasm, devotion, knowledge of [the patron's] mind, and mindfulness [are required]. (VisSd 3.129)
Sweetness, knowledge of humor, and eloquence are its qualities;
these too are classified as superior, inferior, or middling according to their appropriateness.
The hero, the haughty one, the evildoer, and the one in distress are the counter-leaders (*pratināyaka*).
Those factors which kindle the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) are the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*). (VisSd 3.131)
Likewise, the location, time, and so forth of the object of perception manifest an external existence within themselves, awakened by their own respective causes. (VisSd 3.132)
In the world, whatever takes the form of an effect is an *anubhāva* (consequent) in poetry and drama.
The ornaments of women have been described as those born of the limbs and those born of their own nature. *Viśvavidyā-sāra 3.133*.
States of being characterized by that form, as well as other activities and transformations arising from *sattva*, are proclaimed to be *sāttvika*. (VisSd 3.134)
Because they arise solely from the quality of sattva, although distinct in their manifestation, they are:
paralysis, perspiration, horripilation, breaking of the voice, and trembling. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.135)
Change of color, the shedding of tears—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions].
Stupor (*stambha*) is the obstruction of movement caused by fear, joy, disease, and so forth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.136)
The emergence of water from the body is perspiration caused by the heat of passion, fatigue, and so forth;
horripilation is the bristling of the hair caused by joy, wonder, fear, and the like. (VisSd 3.137)
They know that faltering speech (*vaisvarya*) and stammering (*gadgada*) arise from intoxication, exhilaration, affliction, and the like;
trembling of the limbs (*vepathu*) arises from passion, hatred, fatigue, and so forth. (VisSd 3.138)
Change of complexion due to despondency, intoxication, anger, and so forth, is discoloration (*vivarṇatā*).
Tears are the water produced from the eyes, born of anger, sorrow, or joy. (VisSd 3.139)
Dissolution (*pralaya*) consists in the cessation of effort and cognition through pleasure and pain;
it arises from the specific and direct engagement with transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*).
In the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*), there are thirty-three varieties consisting of those that emerge and submerge.
Disgust, agitation, dejection, fatigue, intoxication, and dullness; ferocity, delusion, awakening, sleep, epilepsy, pride, death, lethargy, resentment, sleepiness, dissimulation;

longing, madness, apprehension, together with memory and intelligence; illness, terror, shame, joy, envy, despondency, along with fortitude and fickleness; exhaustion, anxiety, and deliberation. (VisSd 3.141)
Disgust (*nirveda*) arises from the loss of knowledge of reality, envy, and so forth;
it consists of self-contempt and produces wretchedness, anxiety, tears, sighing, pallor, labored breathing, and the like. (VisSd 3.142)

Avega is agitation; therein, that born of rain consists of the contraction of the limbs, while that born of portents consists of the drooping of the limbs, and that born of fire consists of being distressed by smoke and the like. (VisSd 3.143)
From the *rājavidravaja* and other [mantras], there is the employment of weapons, serpents, and so forth;
from the wind [mantra] that causes dust and the like, there is the paralyzing and shaking of elephants and other creatures. (VisSd 3.144)
From the desired arise joy (*harṣa*) and from the undesired sorrow (*śuca*); others are to be understood accordingly.
From misfortune and the like arises lack of vigor (*anaujasya*), dejection (*dainya*), and the production of impurity and so forth. (VisSd 3.145)
Fatigue is the exhaustion resulting from sexual pleasure, traveling, walking, and so forth, characterized by labored breathing, sleep, and the like;
intoxication is born from the consumption of liquor and consists of a mixture of delusion and bliss.
By this [fever], the best person lies down; the middling one laughs and sings; and even the one of inferior nature speaks harshly and weeps. (VisSd 3.147)
Non-comprehension would be a state of dullness caused by seeing or hearing what is desired or undesired;
in that state, there occur such signs as unblinking eyes, gazing fixedly, and remaining silent.
Fury and ferocity arise from such things as valor or offenses;
in that state, there are perspiration, shaking of the head, threatening gestures, blows, and so forth. (VisSd 3.149)
Delusion is a state of mental confusion caused by fear, the onset of suffering, or brooding;
it produces fainting, ignorance, falling down, wandering, loss of sight, and so forth. (VisSd 3.150)
Awakening, which is the arrival of consciousness, results from causes that dispel sleep;
it produces yawning, stretching of the limbs, closing of the eyes, and looking about. (VisSd 3.151)
Dream is the experience of objects by one who has entered into sleep, which brings about anger, agitation, fear, exhaustion, pleasure, pain, and so forth. (VisSd 3.152)

Apasmāra, however, is a derangement of the mind caused by the possession of spirits and the like; it causes falling to the ground, trembling, perspiration, frothing at the mouth, salivation, and so forth. (VisSd 3.153)
Pride (*garva*) is intoxication (*mada*) born from power, prosperity, learning, noble lineage, and so forth;
it causes contempt, playful gestures, the display of one's limbs, lack of discipline, and the like. (VisSd 3.154)
Death by means of arrows and the like results in the renunciation of life through the falling of limbs and so forth;
lethargy arises from fatigue, pregnancy, and the like, while dullness is produced by yawning, smiling, and so forth.

Intolerance toward censure, insult, humiliation, and the like, characterized by stubborn attachment, results in actions such as reddening of the eyes, shaking the head, knitting the brows, and raising one's voice. (VisSd 3.156)
Sleep is the closing of the mind, arising from fatigue, exhaustion, intoxication, and so forth;
it is the cause of yawning, the closing of the eyes, labored breathing, the stretching of the limbs, and other such effects. (VisSd 3.157)

Deceit (*avahitthā*) is the concealment of the outward appearance of joy and so forth due to fear, respect, shame, and the like; it produces activities such as feigning interest in another task, speaking otherwise than one truly feels, and looking away. (VisSd 3.158)
The longing arising from the non-attainment of what is desired consists in an inability to endure the passage of time;
it produces mental distress, agitation, perspiration, long sighs, and so forth. (VisSd 3.159)

Delusion of mind and insanity caused by desire, grief, fear, and so forth, which result in inappropriate laughter, weeping, singing, and prattling; [these are the characteristics of the wind disorder]. (VisSd 3.160)

The apprehension of impending misfortune due to the cruelty of others, one's own faults, and so forth, causes discoloration, trembling, loss of voice, looking toward the sides, and dryness of the mouth. (VisSd 3.161)

Memory is said to be a cognition whose object is a previously experienced thing; it is produced by factors such as similar knowledge and reflection, and by actions such as the raising of the eyebrows. (VisSd 3.162)
Discernment (*mati*) is the determination of meaning through following the path of ethics and so forth;
from that arise cheerfulness, fortitude, contentment, and great respect. (VisSd 3.163)
Disease, such as fever and the like, is caused by the [imbalances of] wind and so forth, producing trembling of the earth and other effects;
terror, produced by thunderclaps, lightning, meteors, and the like, causes shaking and other such phenomena. (VisSd 3.164)

Shame (*vrīḍā*) is the absence of audacity; arising from misconduct, it causes the face to bow down and so forth. Joy (*harṣa*), however, is the clarity of mind resulting from the attainment of the desired; it brings about tears, a faltering voice, and other such signs.
Envy is the intolerance of the excellence of others' virtues due to arrogance;
it manifests through the proclamation of faults, the knitting of eyebrows, contemptuous gestures, anger, and other such signs. (VisSd 3.166)
But despondency, born from the absence of a means, is a depletion of one's vital strength; it causes sighing, gasping, heartache, and the searching for companions. (VisSd 3.167)

Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the fulfillment of one's desires through the attainment of knowledge and so forth; it produces the radiance of speech, laughter, eloquence, and the like, characterized by complete satisfaction. (VisSd 3.168)
Restlessness, however, is instability arising from envy, hatred, passion, and so forth;
in that state, there occur such things as scolding, harshness, and conduct contrary to one's vows.
Fatigue, arising from sexual pleasure, exertion, mental distress, hunger, thirst, and so forth, produces a lack of vitality, trembling, emaciation, lack of enthusiasm, and the like. (VisSd 3.170)
Dhyāna is reflection; because it does not attain what is beneficial, it causes distress and heat through the inhalation of emptiness.
Vitarka is investigation; arising from doubt, it makes the eyebrows, head, and fingers dance. (VisSd 3.171)
Even emotions such as love (rati) may become transitory states (vyabhicārin) in an indefinite rasa;
likewise, laughter is considered [transitory] in the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and heroic (vīra), and anger in the heroic. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.172)
"Repugnance is said to be a transitory state even in the context of tranquility";
thus, other [transitory states] such as this are to be understood by those whose intellects have been cultivated in that manner. (VisSd 3.173)

Whether non-contradictory or contradictory, that state which is incapable of being obscured by them is recognized as the *sthāyibhāva* (the permanent emotion), being the bulbous root from which the sprout of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) emerges. (VisSd 3.174)
Love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust and wonder—thus eight are proclaimed, and tranquility (śama) as well. VisSd 3.175.
*Rati* (love) is the inclination of the mind toward an object agreeable to it;
*hāsa* (laughter) is held to be the expansion of the heart through transformations of speech and other faculties. (VisSd 3.176)

The distress of the mind caused by the loss of what is desired and so forth is designated by the term "sorrow" (śoka). The perception of harshness toward disagreeable objects is held to be "anger" (krodha). (VisSd 3.177)

The intensity of exertion at the commencement of tasks is called steadfast enthusiasm (*utsāha*). Fear (*bhaya*), however, is the agitation of the mind produced by the power of the *raudra* [sentiment]. (VisSd 3.178)
Censure arising from the observation of faults and so forth, as well as that born of wonder, occurs with regard to various objects that transcend the boundaries of the world. (VisSd 3.179)
The expansion of the mind is declared to be wonder (*vismaya*);
tranquility (*śama*) is the bliss born from resting in one's own self during the state of effortless composure.

Because they bring forth aesthetic flavors (rasas) through their connection with various types of dramatic representation (abhinaya), these are called "states" (bhāvas): the stable (sthāyin), the transitory (sañcārī), and the innate (sāttvika).

The erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the loathsome, and the marvelous—these are the eight rasas; likewise, the peaceful (śānta) is considered the ninth. VisSd 3.182.
For the "peak" (*śṛṅga*) is the manifestation of love, caused by that [meeting];
the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that is primarily characterized by an excellent nature is considered to be the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). (VisSd 3.183)

In this context, with the exception of one already married and a courtesan who lacks affection, the heroines—such as the *dakṣiṇā* and others—serve as the objective supports for the hero. (VisSd 3.184)
The moon, sandalwood, the humming of bees, and so forth, are considered the excitants (*uddīpana*);
the movement of the eyebrows, side-long glances, and so forth, are proclaimed to be the ensuants (*anubhāva*). (VisSd 3.185)

Having abandoned the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) of ferocity, death, indolence, and disgust, its stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) is love (rati); this [rasa] is dark-complexioned and has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
It is considered to be of two kinds: the love-in-separation (vipralambha) and the love-in-enjoyment (saṃbhoga). VisSd 3.186.
But where there is intense passion yet the desired object is not attained, that is *vipralambha* (love-in-separation);
and it is of four kinds: consisting of *pūrvarāga* (first love), *māna* (jealous anger), *pravāsa* (separation by distance), and *karuṇa* (sorrow). (Viśvanātha’s Śāradātilaka 3.187)
When passion has taken root between two people through either hearing of or seeing one another,
that particular state which exists before their union is called "preliminary passion" (pūrvarāga).
In that regard, hearing [of the deity] may occur through the mouths of messengers, bards, or female companions;
and there is seeing [the deity] in a magical illusion, in a painting, directly, or in a dream. (VisSd 3.189)
Longing, anxiety, remembrance, recounting virtues, agitation, and lamentation; madness, disease, stupor, and death—these are the ten stages of love. (VisSd 3.190)
Longing is desire; anxiety is the thinking of means for attainment and so forth;
and madness is the lack of discrimination even regarding what is conscious and unconscious. (VisSd 3.191)
Due to the intense wandering of the mind, there may be incoherent speech that cannot be discerned;
as for the physical ailment, it consists of long sighing, paleness, emaciation, and so forth. (VisSd 3.192)

Inertness, the loss of movement in the limbs as well as in the mind, and the cessation of the vital fluids—because these are the causes of death, they are not described [as the signs of siddhi]. (VisSd 3.193)
That which is almost accomplished, as well as that which is desired by the mind, should be expressed;
even if it is merely described, its reanimation will not be far off.

First, the passion of the woman should be expressed, and afterwards that of the man through her gestures. Furthermore, the passion of the first encounter (*pūrvarāga*) is threefold: like indigo, safflower, and madder. (VisSd 3.195)
That love which does not depart from the mind does not shine excessively;
it is called the indigo-dye love, such as that between Śrī Rāma and Sītā.
They call that the safflower-dye which fades yet remains beautiful; they call that the madder-dye which does not fade and shines exceedingly. VisSd 3.197.
Pride and anger are of two kinds, arising from affection and from jealousy; pride born of affection occurs even when there is great joy between the two. (VisSd 3.198)
Because love follows a winding course, there is anger without cause when the husband is seen, inferred, or heard to be in the company of another beloved woman. (VisSd 3.199)
Envy and pride toward women may arise; therein, inference is threefold, occurring through dreaming while awake, signs of enjoyment, and slips of the tongue regarding one's lineage. (VisSd 3.200)

Conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, intimidation, indifference, and a change of sentiment—these are the six expedients a husband should employ in sequence to break her [resistance]. (VisSd 3.201)
In that regard, conciliation consists of pleasant speech; sowing dissension consists of winning over their friends;
bribery consists of giving ornaments and such under a pretext; and prostration consists of falling at one's feet. (VisSd 3.202)
But when the initial [flavor] has completely subsided, there may be the disregard of equanimity;
from impetuosity, fear, joy, and so forth, the loss of anger constitutes another flavor.
Exile consists of being separated from one's country due to a task, a curse, or agitation;
in that state, there is soiling of the limbs and garments, and the head bears a single braid of hair.
Sighing, gasping, weeping, falling to the ground, and so forth arise;
there is a lack of physical grace in the limbs, fever, paleness, emaciation, and loss of appetite. (VisSd 3.205)

Lack of fortitude, being without support, intoxication consisting of that [passion], and fainting, as well as death—these ten stages of Smara (Love) are to be known here in their proper sequence. (VisSd 3.206)
Lack of excellence is the stain of transgression; asceticism is the fever of separation;
lack of relish is detachment from objects; and steadfastness is a lack of passion for everything.
Moreover, emptiness is said to be the mind's lack of an objective support (*anālambanatā*).
For that [emptiness] consists of that [mind], and its manifestation occurs externally and internally.
Therein, that which arises from an effect may be threefold: that which is yet to be, that which is becoming, and that which has already come to be.

When one of two youths has gone to the other world and can no longer be found, and because of that one becomes despondent, that [love] is called "separation through grief" (*karuṇa-vipralambha*). (VisSd 3.209)
Where two lovers, mutually enamored, engage in looking, touching, and so forth, this is declared to be *saṃbhoga*.
Because it is impossible to enumerate its many varieties, such as kissing, embracing, and so forth,
this alone is described by the wise as the erotic sentiment of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*).

In that [state], there may be the six seasons, as well as the moon and sun, their rising and setting, water-sports, strolls in the forest, dawn, drinking wine, the night, and so forth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.212)
One should speak of anointing with ointments, ornaments, and the like, as well as other pure and sanctified things;
this [speech] is said to be of four kinds, beginning with "immediate" (ānantarya) and "prior passion" (pūrvarāga). VisSd 3.213.
The Comic (Hāsya) rasa arises from deceptive behavior such as distorted appearance, speech, dress, and gestures;
its stable emotion is laughter, it is white in color, and its presiding deity is the Pramatha.

When people laugh upon seeing someone whose appearance, speech, and gestures are distorted, they say that person is the objective support (ālambana) here; it is considered that their own behavior serves as the excitant (uddīpana).
The external manifestations (*anubhāva*) are the contraction of the eyes, a smiling face, and so forth;
while sleepiness, lassitude, dissimulation (*avahitthā*), and others may serve as the transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*) in this context. (VisSd 3.216)
For the superior, there are the smile and the laugh; for the middling, the gentle laugh and the loud laugh;
and for the inferior, the derisive laugh as well as the excessive laugh—thus this [laughter] is of six varieties.
The wise have described a smile as having slightly blossoming eyes and quivering lips; laughter is said to be that which reveals a few teeth therein. (VisSd 3.218)
A smile is characterized by a sweet tone; a laugh involves a movement of the shoulders and head;
a derisive laugh has tears in the eyes; and an excessive laugh involves the tossing of the limbs. (VisSd 3.219)
Even if that laughter is not explicitly depicted anywhere,
it is nevertheless perceived through the power of the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors.
Because the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors are perceived without distinction due to their commonality, this comic sentiment (*hāsya-rasa*) is experienced by the audience. (ViśSd 3.221)
From the loss of what is desired and the attainment of what is undesired, the rasa called Karuṇa (Pathos) arises;
this is described by the wise as pigeon-colored and has Yama as its presiding deity.
In this [sentiment], sorrow is the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva); that which is to be mourned is considered the objective basis (ālambana);
furthermore, its states such as burning and so forth would constitute the excitants (uddīpana).

The external manifestations (anubhāvas) include reviling fate, falling to the ground, wailing, and so forth, as well as changes in complexion, heaving sighs, deep breaths, paralysis, and incoherent prattle. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.224)
Disgust, delusion, epilepsy, disease, languor, forgetfulness, fatigue, despondency, dullness, madness, anxiety, and so forth are the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*). (VisSd 3.225)
This rasa is distinct from *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) because its dominant emotion (*sthāyin*) is sorrow;
in *vipralambha*, however, the dominant emotion is love, which is caused by the desire for reunion.
The *raudra* [sentiment] has anger as its underlying emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), is passionate, and has Rudra as its presiding deity;
its objective basis (*ālambana*) is the enemy, and their actions are considered its excitants (*uddīpana*). (VisSd 3.227)
Through the striking of fists, hurling down, mutilation, cutting, and tearing, as well as through the tumult of battle and the like, his blazing [power] becomes intense. (VisSd 3.228)
Frowning of the eyebrows, biting the lips, clapping the arms, threatening gestures, recounting one's own heroic deeds, and brandishing weapons. VisSd 3.229.

The manifestations (*anubhāvas*) are likewise the casting [of glances], cruel looks, and so forth; as well as ferocity, agitation, horripilation, perspiration, trembling, and intoxication. (VisSd 3.230)
In that [heroic sentiment], delusion, indignation, and so forth may be transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*);
however, the redness of the face and eyes here is what distinguishes it from the heroic sentiment of battle (*yuddhavīra*).
The hero of the highest nature has enthusiasm as his dominant emotion;
he is said to have Mahendra as his presiding deity and a golden complexion. (Viśvavidyā 3.232)
The objects of perception (*ālambana*) are considered to be those such as the one to be conquered;
the excitants (*uddīpana*) of that [emotion] consist of the activities of the one to be conquered and so forth;
and the consequents (*anubhāva*) therein would be the seeking of allies and so forth. (VisSd 3.233)
The transitory emotions (sañcārin), however, are fortitude, intelligence, pride, memory, reasoning, and horripilation;
and that [heroism] is fourfold, being endowed with generosity, righteousness, combat, and compassion. (VisSd 3.234)

The *bhayānaka* (terrifying) [rasa] has fear as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), with the spirits (*bhūta*) as its presiding deity; it is characterized by women and those of low nature, and is considered black by those expert in the principles of aesthetics. (VisSd 3.235)
That from which fear arises is considered here to be the objective support (*ālambana*);
furthermore, his most terrible actions constitute the excitant (*uddīpana*).

In this context, the *anubhāva* consists of changes in complexion, faltering speech, fainting, perspiration, horripilation, trembling, looking toward the cardinal directions, and so forth. (Viṣṇu-sādhanā 3.237)
Disgust, agitation, delusion, terror, dejection, wretchedness, apprehension, epilepsy, confusion, death, and so forth are the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*). (ViśSd 3.238)
The aesthetic flavor (rasa) in which disgust is the dominant emotion is called the loathsome (bībhatsa);
it is declared to be blue in color and to have Mahākāla as its presiding deity.
Foul-smelling flesh, blood, and fat are considered the objective support (*ālambana*);
the falling of worms and so forth upon that very [body] is declared to be the intensifier (*uddīpana*). (VisSd 3.240)
Spitting, contorting the face, contracting the eyes, and so forth are considered the consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*) therein; likewise, there may be transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*).

Delusion, epilepsy, agitation, disease, death, and so forth [are the transitory states]; the marvelous [rasa] has wonder as its dominant emotion and has the Gandharvas as its presiding deity. (VisSd 3.242)
The yellow-colored object is considered the support that transcends the world;
furthermore, its greatness as a quality shall be the excitant. (VisSd 3.243)

Stiffness, perspiration, horripilation, faltering voice, agitation, as well as the dilation of the eyes and so forth, are proclaimed to be the secondary emotional manifestations (anubhāvas). // VisSd 3.244 //
The transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as agitation from the force of discursive thought, confusion, and joy, [are present];
the tranquil state, characterized by the stable emotion of peace (śama), is considered the supreme nature.

Having a splendor as beautiful as jasmine and the moon, with Śrī Nārāyaṇa as its presiding deity, it is that which consists of the worthlessness of all things through their impermanence and so forth. (VisSd 3.246)
Alternatively, its object of focus (ālambana) is held to be the nature of the Supreme Self,
as well as sacred hermitages, holy fields of Hari, pilgrimage sites, beautiful forests, and so forth.
The association with great beings and so forth are its excitants (uddīpana);
the physical manifestations such as horripilation are its consequents (anubhāva), and likewise there are the transitory mental states (vyabhicārin). VisSd 3.248.

Disgust, joy, remembrance, extreme fear, compassion, and so forth—because they are of the nature of non-egoism, these are for us [classified as] the heroic (*vīra*) and other sentiments, beginning with compassion (*dayā*). (VisSd 3.249)

For that very tranquility which persists in both the states of union and separation attains the status of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); therefore, in this state, the presence of transitory emotions (*sañcārin*) and the like is not pure.
They know *vatsala* (affection) to be a rasa characterized by manifest wonder;
its stable emotion (*sthāyin*) is affectionate tenderness (*vatsalatā*), and its object (*ālambana*) is considered to be one's son and so forth. (VisSd 3.251)
The excitants (uddīpanas) are its activities, such as learning, heroism, compassion, and so forth;
[the ensuants are] embracing, contact with the limbs, kissing the head, and gazing. (VisSd 3.252)
Thrills, bliss, tears, and so forth are proclaimed as the ensuants (anubhāvas);
while apprehension of the undesirable, joy, pride, and so forth are considered the transitory states (sañcārin). (VisSd 3.253)
The complexion of his body is like the interior of a lotus; the deities are the Mothers of the World.
He is primordial through [the rasas of] compassion, disgust, fury, heroism, and terror.

The Comic sentiment (hāsya) is opposed even to the Terrible (bhayānaka) and the Pathetic (karuṇa); likewise, the Pathetic is similarly opposed by both the Comic and the Erotic (śṛṅgāra) sentiments. (VisSd 3.255)
The Furious [sentiment] is [associated] with the Comic, the Erotic, and the Terrible sentiments;
likewise, the Heroic sentiment is said to be [associated] with the Terrible and the Peaceful.
The peaceful [rasa] is [attained] through those called the erotic, the heroic, the furious, the comic, and the peaceful;
whereas the peaceful is [attained] through the heroic, the erotic, the furious, the comic, and the terrifying.
The opposition between the erotic and the loathsome is thus declared;
for even though [the latter] may, due to some cause, attain stability in a certain context, [it remains opposed]. (VisSd 3.258)

That which is not a stable emotion (*sthāyin*), such as madness and the like, and which does not attain stability in the actor, is a semblance of Rasa or Bhāva; so too are the subsidence and emergence of a Bhāva. (Viśvavidyāsadana 3.259)
Junction (*sandhi*) and variegation (*śabalatā*)—all these are *rasas* because they possess flavor (*rasana*).
The transitory emotions (*sañcārin*) are predominant, as is love (*rati*) directed toward objects such as the gods.
A stable emotion (sthāyī-bhāva) that has merely been awakened is so designated, just as the ingredients such as pepper and sugar pieces become one in a refreshing drink (prapāṇaka). VisSd 3.261.

When there is an excessive manifestation of a particular transitory emotion (sañcārī) in a certain context within a rasa, or when there is an occurrence of impropriety, that constitutes an "appearance" (ābhāsa) of rasa or bhāva. (VisSd 3.262)
In sexual union with a female companion, with the wife of a sage or a guru,
with one's own consort, or likewise in a union that is neither [of these], // VisSd_3.263 //

In the case of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), it is improper [to represent it] when residing in a rival protagonist, or similarly when residing in a low character, an animal, and so forth; in the case of the furious sentiment (*raudra*), it is improper when the anger resides in a teacher or similar superior. (VisSd 3.264)

And when the object of focus is the peaceful, the inferior, the ultimate, or the guru and so forth; or when it is the heroic [mood] directed toward the slaughter of a Brahmin and the like, or toward a base recipient, [then laughter arises]. (VisSd 3.265)
When [the object] has entered an excellent vessel, it should be understood as being terrifying; likewise in other cases.
However, the appearance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) may occur in relation to objects such as courtesans when [the emotion] is shame and so forth. (VisSd 3.266)
In the cessation, arising, junction, and mixture of a state, respectively, the cessation, arising, junction, and variegation of that state are recognized. (VisSd 3.267)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Definition of Rasa and Other Elements," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
(4) The Fourth Chapter.
The determination of *dhvani*:
poetry is considered to be of two kinds—*dhvani* and that in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*).
When the suggested meaning surpasses the expressed meaning, it is *dhvani*; that is the highest form of poetry. (VisSd 4.1)
Two varieties of *dhvani* are also declared, rooted respectively in *lakṣaṇā* (indication) and *abhidhā* (denotation):
one in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣita-vācya*), and the other in which the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate to another (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācya*).
When the expressed meaning is transferred to another sense or is completely set aside,
the *dhvani*— even though its expressed meaning is not intended— is still twofold.
The intended subject matter is also considered to be twofold at the outset:
that in which the suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), and likewise that in which the sequence is perceptible (*lakṣyakrama*). (VisSd 4.4)
[*1] Among those, the first consists of the fundamental forms of denotation; here, the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), emotional states (*bhāva*), and so forth, are counted as only one.
Even though it has a single division, because its varieties are infinite, it cannot indeed be numbered. (VisSd 4.5)

The suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) arising from the power of both word and meaning, which resembles a resonance (anusvāna), is called *dhvani* by the wise; it is threefold, consisting of that where the sequence of suggestion is perceptible (*lakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya*). // VisSd 4.6 //

Because it takes the form of either a fact (vastu) or an ornament (alaṅkāra), that which arises from the power of words (śabda-śakty-udbhava) is of two kinds. Its meaning—whether it be a fact or an ornament—is possible by itself (svataḥ). (VisSd 4.7)

Whether it is infused by the bold assertion (prauḍhokti) of the poet or that of the character portrayed by him—thus there are six [types]. When manifested by those six, however, the suggested object takes the form of either a matter (vastu) or an ornament (alaṅkāra). (VisSd 4.8)
The suggested meaning arising from the power of the sense has twelve varieties;
when added to that which arises from the power of both word and sense, that *dhvani* becomes eighteenfold.
In a sentence, that [suggestion] arising from the power of both word and meaning is considered by the wise to be [the suggestion] in words and sentences;
however, in a literary composition (*prabandha*), it is regarded as the suggestion arising solely from the power of meaning.
In compositions consisting of words, parts of words, syllables, or arrangements, the sequence [of suggestion] is not manifest;
thus, fifty-one varieties of that *dhvani* are recognized. VisSd 4.11.
Through the three types of *saṅkara* (confusion) or through *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) in many ways, [the numbers of verses are] 405, 540, 35, and 535, when calculated with pure [types]. VisSd 4.12.
Furthermore, there is the "subordinate suggested" (guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya) when the suggestion is not superior to the expressed meaning.

In that regard, there may be [the varieties]: that which has the other as its limb (itarāṅga), that which is suggested by intonation (kākvākṣipta), and that which is the suggested meaning for the sake of establishing the expressed (vācya-siddha-vyaṅgya).
With ambiguous predominance, equal predominance, indistinct, unhidden, suggested, and unpleasant—thus its eight varieties have been declared. (VisSd 4.14)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Varieties of Poetry known as Suggestive (dhvani) and that wherein the Suggested Meaning is Subordinate (guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya)," in the *Sāhitya-darpaṇa*. (5)
The fifth chapter:

Since the functions known as denotation (abhidhā), indication (lakṣaṇā), and suggestion (vyañjanā) are exhausted [in explaining the aesthetic experience], a fourth function must be accepted for the cognition of rasa and the like. (VisSd 5.1)

The suggested meaning differs from the expressed meaning due to the distinctions between the cognizer, the nature [of the meaning], number, cause, effect, cognition, time, locus, object, and so forth. (VisSd 5.2)
Since taste and the like do not exist prior [to the contact], the two—indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and naming (*abhidhā*)—are not their cognizers;
furthermore, indication is also absent due to the lack of sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*). (VisSd 5.3)
Inference is not capable of making known suggested elements such as rasa;
nor is the cognition of rasa and so forth a memory, because the reasons [for such an inference] would be fallacious. (VisSd 5.4)
This function, known as *vyañjanā*, is called "suggestion" by the wise;
however, others recognize a further function called "tasting" (*rasanā*) for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (VisSd 5.5)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Function of Suggestion," in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*. (6)
The sixth chapter:
Furthermore, poetry is considered to be of two kinds according to the distinction between the visible and the audible.
Among these, the visible is that which is to be performed; it is called a "rūpaka" (dramatic form) because of the superimposition of its [the original] form upon it. VisSd 6.1.
Mimicry of states is called *abhinaya* (acting), and it is fourfold:
physical (*āṅgika*), vocal (*vācika*), as well as extrinsic (*āhārya*), and likewise internal (*sāttvika*).

The drama (*nāṭaka*), the play (*prakaraṇa*), the monologue (*bhāṇa*), the military spectacle (*vyāyoga*), the mixed drama (*samavakāra*), the heroic drama (*ḍima*), the hunting drama (*īhāmṛga*), the act (*aṅka*), the short scene (*vīthī*), and the farce (*prahasana*): these are the ten types of dramatic compositions (*rūpaka*). (VisSd 6.3)
The *nāṭikā*, *troṭaka*, *goṣṭhī*, *saṭṭaka*, and *nāṭyarāsaka*; the *prasthāna*, *ullāpya*, *kāvya*, *preṅkhaṇa*, and likewise the *rāsaka*. (VisSd 6.4)
The *saṃlāpaka*, the *śrīgadita*, the *śilpaka*, the *vilāsikā*, the *durmallikā*, the *prakaraṇī*, the *hallīśaka*, and the *bhāṇikā*. (VisSd 6.5)
The wise have declared there to be eighteen types of minor dramas (uparūpaka);
it is held that, without distinction, the characteristics of all of them are like those of the drama (nāṭaka).
A drama (*nāṭaka*) should have a well-known plot and be endowed with the five junctures (*sandhi*);
it should possess qualities such as grace (*vilāsa*) and success (*ṛddhi*), and be joined with various manifestations of power (*vibhūti*).
The arising of pleasure and pain is continuous with various flavors;
therein, the numbers beginning with five and ending with ten are proclaimed.

A hero (nāyaka) is considered to be one of renowned lineage, a royal sage (rājarṣi), noble and dignified (dhīrodātta), and powerful; he may be divine, or both divine and non-divine, and is endowed with excellent qualities.
There should be only one predominant sentiment (aṅgin), whether it be the erotic (śṛṅgāra) or the heroic (vīra);
all other sentiments are its subordinates (aṅga), and the marvelous (adbhuta) should be employed in the conclusion (nirvahaṇa).
Four or five principal men occupied with the task [should perform it];
its binding is said to be like the tip of a cow's tail. VisSd 6.11.

It should be characterized by the conduct of perceptible leaders, radiant with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva), with its verbal meaning unhidden, and composed of short, concise verses. VisSd 6.12.
It has an interrupted internal single meaning, contains some slightly connected dots,
is not joined with many functions, and does not possess the withdrawal of the seed-syllable.
Endowed with various methods, it does not contain an excessive number of verses;
it is composed for the sake of essential tasks, both lowly and high.
It is employed through a narrative that cannot be accomplished in a single day;
its central hero is near at hand, and it is joined by three or four dramatic roles.
Calling from afar, killing, battle, the ruin of kingdom, country, and so forth, marriage, eating, the utterance of a curse, death, and likewise sexual union; VisSd_6.16 //
Biting with the teeth, tearing with the nails, and whatever else causes shame;
the drinking from the lower lip while reclining, and the confinement within cities and such.
Free from bathing and anointing with these [unguents], and not too elaborate,
[is the attire] for the retinue of the Goddess and others, as well as for ministers and merchants.

An act (*aṅka*) is defined as that which is endowed with vivid dramatic actions arising from the emotions (*bhāva*) and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), and in which all the characters eventually exit at the end. (Viśvavidyā-sadana 6.19)

That which has entered the "womb" (aṅka), consisting of the stage, the wife, the face, and so forth, is another "act" (aṅka) called the "womb-act" (garbhāṅka); it possesses the seed and is also endowed with the fruit.

In that regard, first is the preliminary stage (pūrvaraṅga), then the worship of the assembly (sabhāpūjā); thereafter follows the narration of the poet’s name and so forth, and then the prologue (āmukha) of the drama.
That which the actors perform before the dramatic subject matter, for the sake of pacifying obstacles on the stage,
is called the *pūrvaraṅga*.
Although its ancillary parts, such as pratyāhāra and the rest, are numerous,
nevertheless the nāndī must certainly be performed for the pacification of obstacles.
Because praise joined with words of benediction is offered to gods,
the twice-born, kings, and others, it is therefore designated as *nāndī*.
It proclaims auspiciousness through the conch, the moon, the lotus, the ruddy goose, and the night-lily;
it is composed of either twelve or eight words.
Having performed the preliminary stage, the director (sūtradhāra) withdraws;
then, having entered, the establisher (sthāpaka) likewise presents the poetic work.

In that [opening], whether celestial or terrestrial, being of a mixed nature or belonging to one of those two, it may indicate the plot, the seed, the introduction, or even the character. (Viśvavidyā 6.27)
Having gratified the audience with sweet verses that indicate the meaning of the poem, he should also proclaim the name and lineage of the poet and the drama. (VisSd 6.28)
And for a certain portion [of the performance], he generally resorts to the *bhāratī* style;
*bhāratī* is the activity of speech based on the actor, consisting primarily of Sanskrit. (VisSd 6.29)
The *prarocanā* (inducement) belongs to the *vīthī*, as do the *prahasana* and the *āmukha*.
Among these, the *prarocanā* consists of making [the audience] eager through praise. (VisSd 6.30)
Where the actress, or the vidūṣaka, or even the pāripārśvika, engage in conversation together with the sūtradhāra; (this is the prastāvanā).

When [the actors] address one another with dialogues arising from their own business that suggest the subject matter at hand, that should be known as the *āmukha* (prologue); it is also called by the name *prastāvanā*.
The *uddhātyaka*, the *kathoddhāta*, the *prayogātiśaya*,
the *pravartaka*, and the *avalagita*— these are the five varieties of the prologue (*prastāvanā*).
When people employ other words to convey the meaning of words whose sense has not yet been understood, that is called *uddhātyaka*. (VisSd 6.34)
If the entry of a character occurs by taking up either the words of the Stage Manager (sūtradhāra) or the meaning thereof, that is called "the introduction of the narrative" (kathodghāta).
If, within a single performance, another performance is employed, and thereby there is an entrance into the vessel, then that is a *prayogātiśaya* (superior performance). // VisSd 6.36 //
Where the holder of the Sūtras describes [the ritual] by relying on the time that has commenced, the entry of the vessel based upon that [time], and that which sets it in motion; // VisSd 6.37 //
When, through the inclusion of one [reason] within another, a different effect is established,
that indeed should be known by the wise as *avalagita* (the "clinging") by name in its formal application.
In this context, the other elements of the *vīthī* should also be employed as they may be available;
likewise, there should be what is spoken on the stage (*nepathyoktam*), what is heard (*śrutam*), and what is speech from the air (*ākāśavacanam*). (VisSd 6.39)
Even when relying [on these], one should employ some one of these varieties of the prologue (āmukha) in dramas and similar works. (VisSd 6.40)
Then, having either seized the object or the vessel, the holder of the thread should exit at the end of the prologue; thereafter, he should perform the main ritual action.
Furthermore, this subject matter is categorized by the wise into two types: one is the primary (adhikārika), and the other is the incidental (prāsaṅgika). VisSd 6.42.
Authority is sovereignty over the fruit, and the possessor of authority is its master;
the narrative concerning that [hero] is called "pertaining to authority" by poets. (Viśvavidyā 6.43)
However, for the sake of its accessories, the *patākā-sthānaka* (the emblematic position) is intended as incidental; it should be employed here after having thoroughly examined the subject matter.

When, while one matter is being considered, another [matter] possessing its characteristic mark is introduced through an adventitious state, that is the *patākā-sthānaka* (the banner-like situation). VisSd 6.45.
The sudden attainment of a meaningful purpose through virtuous qualities by means of figurative expression is proclaimed as this first *patākā-sthānaka*.
Speech that is highly refined, allusive, and based on various poetic compositions—this is proclaimed as the second *patākā-sthānaka*. (Viśvavidyā 6.47)
That which introduces the subject matter, yet remains subtle and modest, and is endowed with a clever reply—this is called the third [type]. (VisSd 6.48)
A well-wrought arrangement of words employed in poetry that possesses a double meaning and suggests another primary sense is the second *patākā-sthānaka*. (VisSd 6.49)
Whatever object may be unsuitable for the hero or for the aesthetic flavor (rasa),
that which is contradictory should be abandoned or otherwise conceived.
That which is not to be seen in its parts, yet is intended to be described; and that discourse which, though arising from two days or more, may extend for as long as a year. (VisSd 6.51)
Furthermore, other matters have been explained at length by the wise through concise summaries and introductory remarks;
however, any object that occurs after a year shall be considered as having arisen below the year.
Whatever business cannot be accomplished during the day at the end of the day should be spoken of by means of "introductions to the plot," having effected a break in the act (aṅkaccheda).
There are five types of introductory scenes (arthopakṣepaka): the *viṣkambhaka*, the *praveśaka*, the *cūlikā*, the *aṅkāvatāra*, and also the *aṅkamukha*. (VisSd 6.54)
The *viṣkambha*, which indicates the portions of the story already narrated and those yet to be told,
is shown at the beginning of an act as a summary of the meaning.
When prepared with the middle [ingredients] or with two middle vessels, it is pure; however, that which is prepared with inferior and middle [ingredients] is considered mixed.

The *praveśaka* (interlude) is to be understood as being performed by low-ranking characters using speech in the anudātta (low) tone, occurring between two acts; the rest is as in the case of the *viṣkambhaka*.
A *cūlikā* (interlude) consists of characters situated behind the curtain (*antar-javanikā*) for the purpose of indicating [future events];
it occurs at the end of an act when characters indicated there are not separated from that act. (VisSd 6.58)
Where this act enters [the stage], it is known as an *aṅkāvatāra*; where there might be a suggestion of all the acts within a single act, that is called an *aṅkāvatāra*. (VisSd 6.59)

They call that the "Act-Introductory" (aṅkamukha), which reveals the meaning of the seed (bīja); it is called "Act-Introductory" because it indicates the subject matter of a broken-off act through the characters at the end of the preceding act. (VisSd 6.60)
When one should display that which is required, that which is to be abandoned, that which is flavorless, and the extensive detail—
then, immediately after the introduction (āmukha), one should show what remains.
In drama, the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) should be employed when characters introduced in the prologue (*āmukha*) appear;
however, this occurs when the plot, being full of aesthetic flavor (*sarasa*), proceeds from its very beginning.
At the very beginning, that [plot] should be established within the *āmukha* (prologue) by means of the *ākṣepa* (introduction) and so forth;
furthermore, the killing of a character of high rank must not be described even through the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) and other such devices.
One should not cause the concealment of one by the other in the case of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) and its constituent elements (vastu).
These [elements] are: the seed (bīja), the drop (bindu), the banner (patākā), the minor episode (prakarī), and the plot-fruit (kārya).
Having understood the five fundamental types of meaning, they should be applied according to the rule;
that which is indicated in a few words spreads out in many ways. (VisSd 6.65)
The primary cause of the fruit is called the seed;
when there is an interruption of the intermediate process, the drop is the cause that prevents its cessation.
An extensive episode that arises incidentally is designated as a *patākā*;
it shall not possess a separate fruit of its own for the hero of the *patākā*. (VisSd 6.67)
When a diversion occurs within the *garbha*, the *sandhi*, or the *vimarśa*, it is considered a *prakarī*; it is an incidental episode situated within a specific part [of the plot]. (VisSd 6.68)
The *prakara* belongs to the hero; it is not his own separate fruit, but rather that which is required as the goal to be accomplished and upon which his undertaking is based.
It is agreed that the completion of that which leads to success must be performed;
there are five stages of an undertaking begun by those seeking its fruit.
Initiation, effort, attainment, hope, certain attainment, and the arrival of the fruit—these constitute the undertaking of zeal for the sake of accomplishing the primary goal. (Viṣṇu-samhitā 6.71)
Effort (prayatna), however, is the activity directed toward the attainment of the fruit, accompanied by great haste;
it consists of the hope for attainment and the possibility of attainment, arising from the apprehension of both means and obstacles. (Viṣṇu-siddhānta 6.72)
Due to the absence of rebirth in the miserable states, attainment is certain; indeed, that state is a definitive attainment.
It would be the union with the fruit, which is the arising of the complete fruit.
However, through their association with these five states in their respective order, the divisions of the plot (itivṛtta) become fivefold,
and there are five junctures (sandhi).
The juncture (*sandhi*) is the connection between two parts that share a single purpose when they occur in succession;
[the five junctures are] the opening (*mukha*), the development (*pratimukha*), the germ (*garbha*), the deliberation (*vimarśa*), and the conclusion (*upasaṃhṛti*).
Thus there are five varieties of this; the definition is stated in order:
that in which the production of the seed occurs through the arising of various meanings and sentiments. (Viśuddhimagga 6.76)
That which is joined with the commencement is proclaimed as the "Mukha" (Opening);
it belongs to the primary means toward the fruit and is situated within the Mukha-sandhi (opening juncture).
