And that where there is a manifestation, as if visible yet invisible, of the primary means to the fruit which had previously begun to emerge, is the "Subsequent" (pratimukha) juncture. (VisSd 6.78)
Where there is the unfolding of the *garbha* (the womb/embryo), accompanied by frequent laughter and searching;
where the primary means to the fruit, having burst forth from the *garbha*, is superior [to it]. (Viṣṇusiddhānta 6.79)
When there is an interruption caused by curses and the like, that is known as the *vimarśa* (the juncture of deliberation).
The elements containing the seed-syllables, such as the opening (*mukha*) and other parts, are scattered according to their respective places. (Viśvavidyāsaṃgraha 6.80)
That is indeed the *Nirvahaṇa* (Conclusion) where various elements are brought together toward a single purpose. [Its components are:
*Upakṣepa* (Introduction), *Parikara* (Development), *Parinyāsa* (Resolution), and *Vilobhana* (Enticement). *Viśvanātha’s Śāradātilaka*, 6.81.
Reasoning, attainment, resolution, application, thorough cultivation,
emergence, performance, and differentiation— these indeed are the limbs at the beginning.

The initial emergence of the subject matter of the poem is known as the *upakṣepa* (the introduction); furthermore, the expansion of that emerged subject matter should be understood as the *parikara* (the elaboration). *Viśvavidyā-sāra*, 6.83.

Its accomplishment is the final conclusion, the proclamation of qualities, the incitement of desire, the thorough deliberation of matters, the application of reasoning, attainment, and the arrival of happiness. (Viśeṣastava 6.84)
The arrival of the seed is called its "concentration" (samādhāna); the purpose produced by pleasure and pain is known as its "application" (vidhāna). VisSd 6.85.
Speech characterized by curiosity is called *paribhāvanā*; the sprouting of the meaning of the seed is *udbheda*, while its further development is *karaṇa*. (Viśeṣastava 6.86)
The commencement of the subject matter, division, breaking apart the compact, playfulness, gliding, shaking, and likewise tormenting; (Viṣṇudharmottara 6.87).
In the *pratimukha* [sandhi], there should be jesting, the splendor of jesting, as well as further exhortation, conflict, and likewise attendance.
Flower, vajra, presentation, and the withdrawal of colors—this exertion for the sake of the enjoyment of passion is called *vilāsa*. (VisSd 6.89)
The pursuit of what is desired and lost is called "wandering about" (parisarpa),
while "shaking off" (vidhuta) is said to be the initial rejection of a proffered conciliation.
That which consists in not perceiving a means [to a goal] is called "torment" (tāpana);
"jesting speech" is "amusement" (narma), while "fortitude" (dhṛti) is that which arises from jesting.
Jesting, radiance, advancing, speech that proceeds in successive reply, contradiction, the onset of misfortune, and the conciliation of one who is angry. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.92)

Attendance may be considered as the flower; a special word is regarded as the diamond (vajra); direct confrontation is the harshness, while a conciliatory approach is the introductory statement. VisSd 6.93.
The approach to the four castes is intended as the withdrawal of the castes;
the path is the bringing forth of what was not [previously manifest], and the sequence is the illustration of forms.
Inclusion (saṅgraha), inference (anumāna), entreaty (prārthanā), and indeed dismissal (kṣipti);
as well as fragmentation (troṭaka), superior force (adhibala), agitation (udvega), and likewise the flight (vidrava) should occur within the *garbha* [section].
In that regard, speech based on deception is considered *abhūtāharaṇa* (the fabrication of the unreal);
the statement of the true meaning is the path; and speech accompanied by deliberation is its form. (VisSd 6.96)
An illustration is said to be a statement endowed with excellence;
the realization of the reality of the nature of things is the sequence, while the compendium is the summary.
The application of conciliation and gifts, as well as the modification [of mantras] based on their characteristics, constitutes inference (anumāna).
Furthermore, the requesting of pleasures, joys, and festivals is what constitutes "prārthanā" (petition).
The disclosure of the secret meaning is *kṣipti*; furthermore, *toṭaka* is speech that is vehement and superior in power, which [occurs] under the guise of a hidden intention. (Viṣṇu-siddhānta 6.99)
Fear arising from kings and the like is proclaimed as *udvega* (agitation);
that which is produced by apprehension, fear, and terror is considered *saṃbhrama* (distress) and *vidrava* (flight).
Denigration, then quarreling, determination, agitation, brilliance, power, attachment, exhaustion, prohibition, and opposition; (Viśuddhimagga 6.101).
In the *vimarśa* (conclusion), there should be *prarocanā* (exhortation), as well as *ādāna* (taking up) and *chādana* (covering);
*doṣaprakhyā* (proclamation of faults) is *apavāda* (reproach), and *saṃpheṭa* is speech of anger. *VisSd* 6.102.
Resolve, however, should be understood as arising from a proposition and a reason;
it is a state of agitation resulting from the transgression against a teacher or from the onset of grief and the like. (Viśeṣastava 6.103)
Threatening and terrifying are proclaimed [as functions]; splendor is further the power (śakti).
The pacification of opposition is "contextual application" (prasaṅga), while the glorification of the Guru is [the function of] praise. 6.104.
Fatigue arising from mental exertion is known as weariness;
the obstruction of a desired object is considered to be frustration. (VisSd 6.105)
The departure due to the completion of the task is known as *virodhana*;
however, *prarocanā* should be understood as that which indicates the purpose of the conclusion. (VisSd 6.106)

They say that "taking up" (ādāna) is the undertaking of a task; furthermore, "concealing" (chādana) is indeed the endurance of insults and the like for the sake of accomplishing that task. (VisSd 6.107)
Reconciliation, awakening, the knot, the decision, the conversation, the composition, favor, bliss, the agreement, and also the embrace. (VisSd 6.108)
Speech, the introductory statement, the conclusion of the poem, and the eulogy—these are to be known by name as the constituent parts of the conclusion. (VisSd 6.109)
The sowing of the seed is the juncture; awakening is the seeking of the task.
Furthermore, the application is the binding together of tasks, while the conclusion is the final determination. *Viśuddhimagga* 6.110.
They say that *paribhāṣaṇa* is the recounting of an experienced object;
a statement made for the purpose of censure is *parivāda*; and *kṛti* is the pacification of an acquired object. *VisSd 6.111*
Service and so forth constitute *prasāda*; bliss is the attainment of what is desired; and the departure from suffering is the *samaya*. That would be the embrace (*upagūhana*).

That which constitutes the attainment of the marvelous—namely, speech consisting of conciliation, gifts, and so forth—is to be understood as the "prior statement" (pūrvavākya), which demonstrates the meaning exactly as it was stated. (VisSd 6.113)
The attainment of the granting of boons is intended as the conclusion of the poem;
whereas the pacification of the king, the country, and so forth is designated as the benediction. (VisSd 6.114)
For this sixty-fourfold auxiliary has been proclaimed by the wise;
one may perform its placement even at an indefinite juncture.
Having observed that it conforms to the aesthetic flavor (rasa), the rasa itself is indeed primary;
for it is the attainment of the wonder of composing the desired subject matter that constitutes the expansion of the narrative.

The attainment of passion, the concealment of those things to be concealed, and likewise the manifestation of those limbs that are to be manifested—these are the sixfold fruit of the application. (Viṣṇusmṛti-sāra 6.117)
Just as a man deprived of his limbs would not be capable of undertaking any enterprise,
so too a poem lacking its constituent parts is unfit for performance.
The hero and the antagonist should perform the subsidiary elements of the junctures;
in their absence, the banner-character (patākā) and others; and in their absence, likewise the rest.
The arrangement of these constituent parts is with a view toward the manifestation of rasa,
and not merely out of a desire to fulfill the requirements of the technical treatises.
However, that conduct which is not contradictory and is highly conducive to the manifestation of rasa and so forth—
even that the wise man might alter or perhaps never speak of at all.
The Kauśikī style is used in the erotic sentiment, the Sāttvatī in the heroic, and the Ārabhaṭī in the furious, the terrible, and the loathsome; the Bhāratī style, however, is employed everywhere.
For these four modes (vṛtti) are the matrices of all drama;
they constitute the specific activities of the heroines and other characters in plays such as the *nāṭaka*.

That [style] which is distinguished by smooth costumes and diverse decorations, crowded with women, abounding in dance and song, characterized by the practice of the arising of sensual enjoyments, and endowed with beautiful grace, is the Kaiśikī. (VisSd 6.124)
Narma, narma-sphūrja, narma-sphoṭa, and narma-garbha are its four limbs; narma is the play of wit. (Viśvadatta 6.125)
That which effects the winning over of beloved persons is also considered to be threefold:
that performed with pure laughter and that consisting of amorous passion (*śṛṅgāra*). (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 6.126)
A "burst of jest" (*narma-sphūrja*) is a new union that begins with pleasure and ends in fear;
a "burst of laughter" (*narma-sphoṭa*) is considered to have little aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), as it is indicated merely by slight traces of emotion (*bhāva*).
The conduct of a leader who proceeds in disguise is characterized by humor and inner gravity;
it is predominantly *sāttvatī*, abounding in goodness, heroism, renunciation, compassion, and uprightness.
The joyful, the trivial-amorous, the sorrowless, and likewise the marvelous;
then the inciting, the composite, the conversational, and the transformative. (VisSd 6.129)
These four are proclaimed as the *viśeṣas* of Sāttvatī:
the one that causes provocation toward the enemy and the one that incites speech. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.130)

The breaking of a collective through the combined power of mantras, meanings, deities, and so forth, is a "conversational" (saṃlāpa) [mantra]; it consists of profound speech and relies upon various states of being. (Viṣṇusiddhānta 6.131)
The "transformer" (*parivartaka*) is the performance of other tasks than those already commenced, through activities such as illusions, magic, battle, anger, or agitation. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.132)
The *uddhatārabhaṭī* (boisterous and violent) is considered to consist of killing, binding, and so forth;
it includes the provocation of objects (*vastūtthāpana*), the clash (*saṃpheṭa*), the contraction (*saṃkṣipti*), and the casting down (*avapātana*). (VisSd 6.133)
Thus, these four varieties of Ārabhaṭī have been proclaimed.
The production of an object brought forth by means of illusion (māyā) and so forth is called *vastūtthāpana*. VisSd 6.134.
*Saṃpheṭa*, however, is a violent clash between two enraged beings; *saṅkṣiptā* is the concise composition of a subject by means of the arts or otherwise. (VisSd 6.135)
The contraction [of the eyes] occurs upon the cessation of the movement; the leader's grasping of another eye [occurs] during entry, fear, exit, joy, and flight. (VisSd 6.136)

"Throwing down" (avapātana) has been mentioned previously; the very same speech that was [previously] stated is here considered "aside" (svagata) when it refers to a matter that must not be heard by others. (VisSd 6.137)
That which is audible to all should be performed openly; that would be an *apavārita* (aside).
However, that which is revealed by turning away from another is a secret (*rahasya*).
When one excludes others with the *tripatāka* hand gesture and converses privately with another, that which occurs within the presence of people is called *janāntika*.
"What do you say?"—when this is employed in a drama without an actor, it is called "speech to the air" (ākāśabhāṣita), even though its meaning is heard although not spoken. (Viśvadha 6.140)
One should display the names of Senā, Dattā, Siddhā, and the courtesans;
likewise, those of merchants, male servants, and female servants who are mostly ready to give. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.141)
Whatever may be the name of the subject matter described in the spring season and so forth, that name should be made the title of the drama, revealing its underlying meaning. (VisSd 6.142)
The designation [of works] such as *prakaraṇas* and so forth is derived from the description of the heroine and the hero;
likewise, *nāṭikās*, *saṭṭakas*, and others are distinguished by their heroines. (VisSd 6.143)

Generally, the causative form of the root *gam* (to go), preceded by *adhi*, is employed in place of [the simple verb] for the word "king": as *svāmī* (master) and *deva* (god) by servants, and as *bhaṭṭa* by those of lower status. (Viśuddhimagga 6.144)
He should be addressed as "friend" by royal sages and likewise by the *vidūṣaka*;
he should be addressed as "O King" by other sages, and also by means of a patronymic suffix denoting his offspring.

A Brahmin Vidūṣaka may be addressed by other Brahmins according to his own wish with their names, or as "Ārya" by others; however, he should be addressed by the king either as "Vayasya" or by his name.
The actress and the stage-manager should address each other by the title "Ārya";
the assistant (pāripārśvika) should address the stage-manager as "Bhāva."
The Sūtradhāra addresses those of equal status as "māriṣa" or "haṇḍe";
he addresses superiors as "vayasya"; middling persons as "haṃho"; and an elder brother as "ārya. (Viśvadatta 6.148)
All those who possess the marks of a divine seer (devarṣi) should be addressed as "Bhagavan.
Furthermore, the Vidūṣaka should address both the queen and the maidservant as "Bhavatī."
O long-lived one! O charioteer! O elder! O father!—thus does one address another; or a son [addresses his father] by name, by clan, or as "child," "little son," or "father. (VisSd 6.150)
A disciple or a younger brother should be addressed as "amātya" or "ārya" by those of lower status;
however, by Brahmins, he is called "amātya" or "saciva."
The wise say that one who is ascetic and tranquil is called "Sādhu";
he is to be honored by disciples and others, being addressed by the name he has assumed for himself. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.152)
One should address a preceptor as "Upādhyāya," an ācārya as "Mahārāja," a sovereign as "Bhūpati," a crown prince as "Svāmī," and a young prince as "Bhartṛdāraka."
A prince should be addressed by his subjects as "O auspicious and gentle-faced one," while a princess, the daughter of her husband, should be addressed as "O lady. (VisSd 6.154)

Women should be addressed by their husbands according to whether they are superior, middling, or inferior: a wife equal [in status] is called "halā," a servant girl "hajje," and likewise a courtesan "ajjukā. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.155)
The courtesan should be addressed as "O Mother," and the elderly woman should be honored by people with such terms of address;
likewise, heretics should be addressed by those who have entered their own religious orders with the appropriate designations.
Śākya and others may be addressed by names such as Bhadradatta;
[the name] should correspond to whatever one's occupation, craft, knowledge, or even caste may be.
He should be addressed by that very name, and others should be known [to be addressed] as is appropriate;
for men who are not base and who have refined themselves, the Sanskrit language should be used.
The Saurasenī [Prakrit] should be employed for such women;
however, one should employ Mahārāṣṭrī in the gāthās of these very same women.
Herein, the Māgadhī language is said to be that of those who move within the king's inner apartments;
the Ardhamāgadhī is that of servants, princes, and merchants. (VisSd 6.160)
In the east, the women of Avanti belong to rogues such as Vidūṣakas;
for those who sport, such as Yodhas and Nāgarikas, there are indeed women from the south.
One should employ the Śābarī [language] for the Śabaras, the Śakas, and others;
the Vāhlīkī for the Vāhlīkas and Māṣas; and the Drāviḍī for the Drāviḍas and those to the north.

Likewise, among the Ābhīras there is the Ābhīrī; among the Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, and others, there is the Caṇḍālī and the Pukkasi; and among those who subsist on wooden vessels, there is also the Śābarī.
Likewise, among charcoal-burners and the like, there may be the Paiśācī, the speech of the Piśācas;
and even among servants who are not of low status, there may be the Saurasenikā.
For children, eunuchs, those under the influence of low planets,
the insane, and the diseased, that [Prakrit] itself should be used, though sometimes Sanskrit may be employed.
For one who is intoxicated by power and for one who is afflicted by poverty, as well as for those wearing robes of bark and so forth, one should employ the ordinary [mantra]. (VisSd 6.166)
Sanskrit should be employed with women of high caste and those who bear religious marks;
some have likewise stated that it may be used with queens, the daughters of ministers, and courtesans. VisSd 6.167.
Furthermore, according to the requirements of the task, there should be a reversal of the languages used by those of superior and other ranks.
For the sake of displaying wit, one should employ Sanskrit from time to time when addressing women, female friends, children, courtesans, gamblers, and celestial nymphs.
In this [work], there are thirty-six characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the ornaments of drama (*nāṭyālaṅkāra*);
thirty-three [elements] are to be employed, along with the thirteen components of the *vīthī*. (VisSd 6.170)
The ten limbs of *lāsya* are to be employed as available, in accordance with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*):
ornamentation (*bhūṣaṇa*), clusters of syllables (*akṣara-saṅghāta*), beauty (*śobhā*), and likewise illustration (*udāharaṇa*). (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 6.171)
The reason, doubt, and the example; equal reasoning, the collection of words; the intended meaning of the illustration, attainment, and indeed investigation. VisSd 6.172.
Likewise, there are the excellence of qualities as taught by destiny, as well as their deficiency;
the qualifications and etymologies, and the success, failure, and reversals.
Civility, conciliation, the sense of a garland, presumption, as well as censure, inquiry, renown, similarity, brevity, and the praise of virtues. (VisSd 6.174)
A trace, a wish, the accomplishment of what was not spoken, and likewise pleasant speech—these are the characteristics;
conjunction with qualities accompanied by ornaments is the embellishment. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.175)

Wherein an unestablished meaning is revealed together with established meanings, through a combination of descriptive syllables consisting of measured, variegated words; [that is a *samasyā*]. (VisSd 6.176)

That is called "beauty" (śobhā), wherein the meaning is characterized by wordplay and metaphorical suggestion (śliṣṭa-lakṣaṇa-citra-artha) through the demonstration of a sentence joined with a similar sense. (VisSd 6.177)
When the intended object is established, that is considered an example;
a statement that briefly expresses the reason is held to be a probans because it demonstrates the cause for what is desired.
Doubt is the lack of certainty regarding a statement for one who has not ascertained the truth;
an example (dṛṣṭānta), however, is an illustration presented for the sake of establishing the meaning of the subject (pakṣa).

When a logical argument (tarka) is consistent with the meaning that conforms to the fundamental nature (prakṛti), and when there is a collection of words corresponding to that meaning, that is called *padoccaya* (the accumulation of words). (VisSd 6.180)
Where there is a detailed exposition of well-known facts for the purpose of refuting the positions of others, that is called an illustration (nidarśana). VisSd 6.181.
The intention [of this] is that there is a conceptualization of a non-existent object due to similarity;
it is an attainment when something is inferred through some particular aspect.
Investigation (*vicāra*) is the perception of an object not currently present through reasoning and scriptural statements;
its description according to place, time, and essential nature is called "instruction" (*diṣṭa*). (VisSd 6.183)
The captivating speech taught in accordance with the scriptures should be applied;
however, one must act so as to transcend the [mere] qualities, for that which pertains to the qualities is the opposite.
That which is an abundance of common qualities is considered an excellence of quality (*guṇātiśaya*).
Having stated many established facts, a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is a statement of distinction (*viśeṣokti*). (VisSd 6.185)
The statement of a matter already established is called *nirukti*;
the recitation of many [names] is *siddhi* for the sake of accomplishing the intended purpose. (VisSd 6.186)
For the arrogant and others, there is a fall from existence; speech is either [true] or otherwise than what is spoken;
the state of deliberation is otherwise [than certainty]; but from doubt, there is error.
Courtesy is the conformity to the minds of others through gesture and speech;
conciliation with affectionate words should be the means for accomplishing one's purpose. (Viśuddhimagga 6.188)
A *mālā* (garland) would be that which, for the sake of a desired object, establishes multiple meanings;
*arthāpatti* (presumption) is when another meaning is understood from the statement of one meaning. (ViSd 6.189)
But in the proclamation of a fault, there is intimidation; that is censure.
Seeking the meaning through questions by means of other entreaties is considered inquiry. (VisSd 6.190)
Establishment [of the deity] is the accomplishment of the goal by means of objects well-known in the world that are excellent;
conformity is the increase of agitation through the conformity of that which is appropriate.

That which is a summary is so called because it is condensed; that which is the proclamation of qualities is precisely the "proclamation of qualities" (guṇakīrtana) when it is applied to an object other than the self. (VisSd 6.192)
A statement preceded by a resemblance is called *leśa* (an ellipsis);
whereas *manoratha* is the expression of an intention by means of an indirect manner of speech.
The expansion of specific meanings and the establishment of what was not explicitly stated are proclaimed;
pleasant speech is that which, being uttered with joy, serves to lead the venerable one [to act]. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.194)
Blessings, lamentation, feigned indignation, pride, exertion, refuge, derision, longing, agitation, remorse, and attainment; // VisSd_6.195 //
Aspiration and determination are designated as "spreading" (visarpa) and "scratching" (ullekha);
incitement, censure, policy, and the specification of purpose [are other types]. (VisSd 6.196)
Encouragement, assistance, esteem, compliance, praise, responding to requests as they arise, avoidance [of harm], and reporting [one's own faults]. (VisSd 6.197)
Commencement, narration, reasoning, and exhilaration—these are the dramatic ornaments (*nāṭyālaṅkṛti*), which serve as the causes for the embellishment of drama (*nāṭyabhūṣaṇa*). (VisSd 6.198)
*Āśis* is the wishing for the welfare of a beloved person; *ākranda* is the lamentation of one in grief;
and *kapaṭa* is that wherein another form is manifested through illusion (*māyā*). (VisSd 6.199)
Intolerance is that which cannot endure even the slightest insult;
it is speech born of pride and arrogance, and exertion at the commencement of an undertaking.
Acquisition is said to be the basis for the sake of accomplishing virtuous goals;
whereas derision is a mockery directed at one who is unvirtuous yet conceives themselves to be virtuous.
That longing which arises from the desirability of an object is indeed *spṛhā* (covetousness).
On the other hand, that which consists of uttering words of revilement is declared to be *kṣobha* (agitation). VisSd 6.202.
That very remorse for an object disregarded through delusion is considered "upapatti" (logical justification);
it is the presentation of a reason for the sake of establishing the point. (VisSd 6.203)
Āśaṃsana is the same as āśaṃsā; pratijñā is that which involves determination.
Visarpa is an undertaking that yields undesirable results. (VisSd 6.204)
The mention of a task is intended as a reminder or an incitement;
it is a harsh speech used for the purpose of accomplishing one's own business by urging another to action. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.205)
Reproach is censure; policy is conduct according to the scriptures;
and it is the manifold repetition of a matter already stated. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.206)
Through a specific censure, there may be a specific qualification of the object;
through words of encouragement, there may be the application of someone to exertion. (VisSd 6.207)
Whatever assistance there may be in times of distress and whatever favor one shows toward another, that indeed is pride; following [others] out of humility is the opposite of that.
Continuity is considered to be the narration of past deeds and their glorification;
while entreaty is any request made either personally or through the mouth of a messenger.
Expiation (*parihāra*) is said to be the cleansing of what has been improperly done;
whereas reporting (*nivedana*) is the communication of neglected duties. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.210)
The "incitement" (pravartana) is that which is a virtuous exhortation toward action;
"narrative" (ākhyāna) is the telling of past events; and "reasoning" (yukti) is the ascertainment of the meaning. (VisSd 6.211)
Exultation is the heightening of joy; instruction is the act of teaching.
The sung verse (*geya-pada*) consists of recitation while standing, recitation while seated, and the *puṣpa-gaṇḍikā*. (Viśuddhimagga 6.212)
The *pracchedaka*, the *trigūḍha* known as *saindhava*, the *dvigūḍha*, the *uttamottamaka*, and also the *uktapratyukta*. (Viśvavidyā 6.213)
Indeed, these ten types of limbs have been taught by the wise for the *lāsya* dance;
they are performed while seated upon a throne with a stringed instrument placed before one.

Pure singing (*śuddha-gāna*) is said to be the sung verse (*geya-pada*) and the fixed recitation (*sthita-pāṭhya*); therein, one who is tormented by passion (*madana*) stands and recites in the Prakrit language.
Deprived of all musical instruments, with women overcome by grief and anxiety,
and with their bodies unadorned, it remained exactly as it had been when they were seated.
Song accompanied by musical instruments, various meters, the inverted behavior of men and women, and clusters of flowers. (VisSd 6.217)
Considering her husband to be attached to another woman, a woman’s singing preceded by the lute out of the anger of severed love is known as *pracchedaka*. (VisSd 6.218)
The dance of men wearing female attire is smooth and possesses three secrets;
it may involve someone who has missed a rendezvous and is accompanied by clearly manifest gestures.
Where one speaks in the vernacular language, that is considered Saindhava;
it is a song with square verses, endowed with the *mukha* and *pratimukha* sections.

Furthermore, the *uttamottamaka* (the highest of the high) is doubly profound, rich in rasa and bhāva, capable of producing both anger and favor, and characterized by invective yet supreme in rasa. (VisSd 6.221)

It is endowed with gestures and playful coquetry, captivating through its various poetic compositions, joined with dialogue and counter-dialogue, and characterized by reproach as if it were untrue. (VisSd 6.222)

When this very same dialogue of questions and answers, consisting of the meaning of songs endowed with graceful charm, is performed together with all the *patākā-sthānaka*s, it is called [the *vilāsa*]. (VisSd 6.223)
The wise have declared that a Mahānāṭaka consists of ten acts;
in a Prakaraṇa, the plot should be worldly and invented by the poet.
In the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the hero (*nāyaka*) is a brahmin, a minister, or a merchant;
he is devoted to dharma, kāma, and artha that may involve danger, and is steadfast and tranquil. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.225)
The heroine may be of noble birth in some cases, a courtesan in others, or both in some instances;
thus there are three varieties of it, of which the third is the variety in question.

The *bhāṇa* is crowded with gamblers, dice-players, and other parasites such as jesters and servants; it depicts the conduct of rogues and consists of various shifting states of affairs. (VisSd 6.227)
In this [performance], there is a single actor who is alone, skillful, learned, and a wit;
he should manifest on the stage what has been experienced by himself or by another.
One should carry out the calls and responses through voices from the sky;
one should indicate the heroic and erotic sentiments through descriptions of valor and beauty. (Viśvavidyā 6.229)
In that [type of drama], the plot is based on historical events, the style is generally *bhāratī*,
and it contains the two junctures (*saṃdhi*) of the opening (*mukha*) and the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*), as well as all ten components of the *lāsya* dance.

The *vyāyoga* is well-known for its plot based on past events, involves a small number of female characters, lacks the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures, and is populated by many men. (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 6.231)
It shall consist of a single act, have women as its motif, and conclude with the arrival of the gods;
it is devoid of the Kaiśikī style, and its hero is well-known. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.232)
Whether he be a royal sage or a celestial being, and whether he be firm or haughty,
the primary sentiments (*rasas*) in this context are those other than the comic, the erotic, and the peaceful.
In the *samavakāra*, however, the plot is well-known and concerns the gods and asuras;
it has three acts, and its junctures (*sandhi*) are without pauses (*nirvimarśa*). (VisSd 6.234)
Likewise, there are two joints at the ends, and again one each [in between];
the twelve leaders are renowned as gods and humans endowed with the udātta accent.
Their fruits are each distinct; all the sentiments (rasa) are present, with the heroic as the foremost;
the dramatic styles (vṛtti) are predominantly the gentle (manda-kaiśikī); and neither the *bindu* nor the *praveśaka* occurs here.
And there should be thirteen constituent parts of the street (vīthy-aṅga) as they may be obtained; and here there are various meters (chandas), beginning with Gāyatrī and Uṣṇih. (Viṣṇu-saṃhitā 6.237)
This first act, characterized by three amorous gestures, three deceptions, and three kinds of cries, is to be accomplished through twelve nāḍīs of time. (Viśvāvasu’s Śṛṅgāratilaka 6.238)

In the second act, by means of four [verses], and in the third act, by means of two; the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is threefold—consisting of dharma, artha, and kāma—and furthermore, there is deception (kapaṭa). VisSd 6.239.
Furthermore, flight may be natural or artificial, and caused by fate;
it may be produced by inanimate things, by animate beings, or by both animate and inanimate things combined.

The *ḍima* is characterized by a preponderance of magical illusions, Indra’s net, battles, the agitated behavior arising from anger, and intense passions; its plot is based on a well-known historical event. (VisSd 6.241)

The heroic sentiment (raudra-rasa) is the primary element there, while all other sentiments are subordinate; furthermore, four acts (aṅka) are prescribed for it, and neither the interlude (viṣkambhaka) nor the introductory scene (praveśaka) is used here.
The leaders— the gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and mahoragas,
as well as the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and so forth— numbering sixteen, were exceedingly arrogant.

The *vṛttis* should be devoid of *kaiśikī*, and the junctures (*sandhi*) should be without deliberation (*nirvimarśa*). The sentiments (*rasa*) should be the six [flavors], excluding the peaceful (*śānta*), the comic (*hāsya*), and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.244)
The *īhāmṛga* is proclaimed to have a mixed structure and four constituent parts (*aṅgas*);
its junctures (*sandhis*) are the *mukha*, *pratimukha*, and likewise the *nirvahaṇa*.
The hero and the counter-hero are known as Nara and Divyāvani-Yama;
both are *dhīroddhata* (firm and haughty), while the other [the third] is firm and haughty due to his hidden nature and his performance of improper acts.

Even for one who does not desire to abduct her by force when she is unwilling, one should display here and there some semblance of amorous passion toward that divine woman. (Viṣṇu-sahasranāma-ṭīkā 6.247)
The ten divine or human leaders of the banners, having brought about a fierce battle with great fury, withdraw under a pretext. (VisSd 6.248)
"Even if they have reached the point of execution, these great-souled ones should not be put to death by us here," they said;
yet others, however, declared, "The Lord alone is the sole witness here, not we. (Viṣṇuśataka 6.249)
The battle caused by a celestial woman, the six leaders, and others;
the *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* has one act, and its protagonists are common men. *VisSd* 6.250.
In this [drama], the sentiment is the pathetic (karuṇa), with lamentation by many women as the stable emotion;
the poet should mentally elaborate upon the well-known narrative. (VisSd 6.251)

In this [debate], the elements of connection, style, and the members [of the syllogism], victory and defeat, and the battle must be conducted through speech; there should be much talk of renunciation. *Viśeṣastava* 6.252.
In the street scene (vīthī), there may be a single character; here, a certain individual is postulated who relies on various replies expressed through speeches directed at empty space (ākāśabhāṣita).
It should indicate abundant erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) while pointing toward the other sentiments (*rasa*) slightly;
[it should contain] the opening (*mukha*) and concluding (*nirvahaṇa*) junctures (*sandhi*), as well as all the dramatic elements (*arthaprakṛti*). (VisSd 6.254)
The wise point out that this [drama] has thirteen components:
the *uddhātyaka*, the *avalagita*, the *prapañca*, the *trigata*, and the *chala*. (Viśvadha 6.255)
When the power of speech is excessive, there is a swelling of the cheeks and a drooping of the lips;
furthermore, these consist of idle chatter, improper talk, and softness.

Mutual discourse that is unreal is considered to be frivolous chatter (*prapañca*) intended for laughter; it may involve three points and consist of the application of multiple meanings through the similarity of sounds. (VisSd 6.257)
"Chala" (quibble) consists of enticing and deceiving someone with words that are either pleasant or unpleasant;
others, however, say that "chala" is when one directs someone toward a particular task. (VisSd 6.258)
That speech which is uttered through deceit, laughter, or anger is "verbal play" (*vākkelī*);
it arises from two or three exchanges connected with laughter. (VisSd 6.259)

The utterance of mutually excessive speech out of rivalry is considered *adhibala*. *Gaṇḍa* is speech that is connected to the subject at hand, yet possesses a different meaning and is delivered with haste. (VisSd 6.260)
An explanation that deviates from what was stated according to its own natural sense becomes a distortion;
it is like a riddle joined with laughter, which is merely a "nālikā."
Idle chatter is speech that is incoherent or whose reply is likewise disconnected, as well as beneficial words spoken in the presence of a fool who does not comprehend them. (Viśeṣastava 6.262)
Speech that, for the sake of another, causes laughter or agitation, wherein virtues appear as faults and faults as virtues—that indeed is frivolity. (VisSd 6.263)

A *prahasana* (farce) should be composed with the *bhāṇa* style, including the junctures (*sandhi*), the members of the junctures (*sandhyaṅga*), and the members of the dance (*lāsyāṅka*), and its plot should consist of characters conceived by the poet who are objects of censure. *Viśvavidyāsadana* 6.264.
In this [play], there is neither the *ārabhaṭī* style nor the *viṣkambhaka* or *praveśaka* scenes;
the predominant sentiment (*rasa*) therein is the comic (*hāsya*), nor is there the presence of the constituent elements (*vīthy-aṅga*) of the minor plot.
When the hero alone among ascetics, the Blessed One, brahmins, and others is impudent therein, it is called pure comedy (śuddha-hāsya);
when he relies upon some other person, they know that as mixed (saṅkīrṇa).
Some have stated that the *vṛtta* of many [syllables] is "mixed" (*saṅkīrṇa*) when it consists of two parts or is constructed with a single part. (VisSd 6.267)
But they know that which is "transformed" (vikṛta) to be where eunuchs, chamberlains, and ascetics appear,
endowed with the dress and speech of libertines, actors, soldiers, and the like.

A *nāṭikā* should have an invented plot, consist mostly of female characters, and contain four acts; its hero should be a renowned king of the *dhīralalita* (calm and playful) type. *Viśvavidyā-sāra*, 6.269.
The heroine here, born of a royal lineage, may be one connected with the inner apartments, or engaged in music, or a maiden possessed of fresh passion. (VisSd 6.270)
The leader might not proceed with her out of fear and apprehension;
however, the queen would be senior, bold, and born of a royal lineage. (VisSd 6.271)
At every step, the union of the two should be under her control, as she possesses a sense of pride;
the style (vṛtti) should be Kaiśikī, and the junctures (sandhi), moreover, should involve little deliberation.
They say that a *troṭaka* consists of seven, eight, nine, or five acts, is based on both the divine and the human realms, and contains a *saṃvidūṣaṇa* in every act. (Viśvanātha’s Śāradātilaka 6.273)
A social gathering (goṣṭhī) adorned by nine or ten ordinary men, lacking noble speech and characterized by the Kaiśikī style of performance, [is not a true assembly]. (VisSd 6.274)
It is inferior due to the deliberation on the womb; it should be composed of five or six women, joined with love and the erotic sentiment, and fashioned as a single act.

A *saṭṭaka* should consist entirely of Prakrit dialogue, lack any *praveśaka*, and likewise contain no *viṣkambhaka*; furthermore, the predominant sentiment (*rasa*) therein is the marvelous (*adbhuta*). (VisSd 6.276)
The acts (aṅkas) are called "curtains" (javanikā); otherwise, it is similar to a nāṭikā.
The Nāṭya-rāsaka consists of a single act and is established with many tālas and layas.
Likewise, it has a noble hero and a *pīṭhamarda* as a secondary hero;
here, the comic sentiment (*hāsya*) is subordinate, while the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) is primary, and the heroine is one who has prepared herself for the tryst.
In the *mukha* (opening) and *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion), there are all ten *lāsyāṅgas* (elements of dance).
Some, however, do not desire the *pratimukha* (development) juncture here at all.
In the *prasthāna* [mode], the hero is a servant (*dāsa*) and the subordinate hero (*upanāyaka*) is likewise lowly;
the heroine (*nāyikā*) is a female servant (*dāsī*), and the styles (*vṛtti*) are *kaiśikī* as well as *bhāratī*. (VisSd 6.280)
From the application of drinking liquor, there is the withdrawal of the intended object;
likewise, there are two gestures (*aṅka*), dissolution, rhythm (*tāla*), and so forth, as well as abundant graceful movement (*vilāsa*).
It has a noble hero, a divine plot, and is adorned with a single act;
it is endowed with the elements of the *śilpaka* and the sentiments (*rasa*) of humor, love, and pathos.
It is to be performed with many battles and is enchanting with songs of weaponry;
some say there are four heroines and three acts therein. (VisSd 6.283)

The *kāvya* (dramatic performance) is devoid of the *ārabhaṭī* style, consists of a single act (*ekāṅka*), is filled with humor (*hāsya*), and is adorned with *vipadikā* and *bhagnatāla* rhythms, as well as *khaṇḍa* measures. (VisSd 6.284)

Accompanied by the abandonment of syllables and morae, it contains erotic speech; here the hero and the heroine are noble, and the first two as well as the last junctures [of the plot] are likewise so. (Viśvāvasu-śāstra 6.285)

It is devoid of the *garbhāvamarśa* juncture, lacks a swinging stage (*preṅkhaṇa*), has a low-ranking protagonist, lacks a stage director (*sūtradhāra*), consists of a single act (*ekāṅka*), and is without *viṣkambha* or *praveśaka* scenes. (VisSd 6.286)
In that [performance], the *nāndī*— which involves wrestling and combat and is based on all dramatic styles (*vṛtti*)— is sung in the *nepathya* (tiring room), as is the *prarocanā*.

The Rāsaka should consist of five characters and be endowed with the Mukha and Nirvahaṇa sandhis; it abounds in various languages and dialects and is characterized by the Bhāratī and Kaiśikī vṛttis. (Viśvadatta 6.288)

It should lack a stage director, consist of a single act, include the elements of a vīthī, and be endowed with artistic skill; it should possess a clever *nāndī* benediction, feature a renowned heroine, and have a foolish hero. (VisSd 6.289)
Some also declare that the *pratimukha* juncture consists of the successive arrangement of exalted states (*udātta-bhāva*). (Viśvavidyā 6.290)
In the *saṃlāpika*, there are four or three acts; furthermore, the hero is a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*), and the sentiment therein is primarily the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*).
In cases of siege of the city, treacherous battle, or flight,
neither the Vṛtti nor the Kaiśikī style of dramatic composition is appropriate there.

It should have a well-known plot, consist of a single act, feature a renowned and noble hero, and include a famous heroine; it must be devoid of the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures. (Viśvavidyā 6.293)
An *uparūpaka* consisting largely of the *bhāratī* style and abounding with the word "glory" (*śrī*) is known by the learned as the *mata*, which is said to be "glorious" (*śrīgadita*). (VisSd 6.294)
Some declare that when Śrī is seated, one should sing what has been spoken by Śrī or even recite something; this is called the *ekāṅka*, which consists mostly of *bhāratī* style. (VisSd 6.295)
In the Śilpaka, there should be four acts and likewise four styles;
the sentiments are the Furious and the Comic, and the hero is considered to be a Brāhmaṇa.
In this [work], the description of the cremation ground and so forth may be deficient; the secondary hero (upanāyaka) should be present.
Its constituent parts (aṅgas), moreover, are twenty-seven. (ViSd 6.297)
Hope, deliberation, doubt, distress, agitation, attachment, effort, composition, longing, dissimulation, and comprehension; (Viṣṇu-siddhi 6.298)
Graceful playfulness, languor, tears, intense joy, sighs of relief, bewilderment, as well as the attainment of confidence, perseverance, encouragement, and wonder; VisSd_6.299.
Gain, forgetfulness, agitation, fearlessness, awakening, and wonder—since these are self-evident, their defining characteristics are not stated here. (VisSd 6.300)
Abounding in the erotic sentiment, consisting of a single act, endowed with the ten limbs of *lāsya*, and adorned by the *vidūṣaka*, the *viṭa*, and the *pīṭhamarda*. (VisSd 6.301)
Deficient in both the examination of the womb and the two joints, with a deficient leader, very small in stature, and well-adorned—she is known as the Vilāsikā. (VisSd 6.302)

The *durmallī* should have four *aṅkas*, be endowed with the *kaiśikī* and *bhāratī* styles, lack a *garbha* (interlude), feature city-dwellers as its characters, and be adorned by a subordinate hero. *Viśvavidyā-sādhana* 6.303.
The first act of this [play] should consist of three *nālikās* and be filled with the amorous play of a *viṭa*;
the second act, possessing five *nālikās*, should be full of the dalliance of a *vidūṣaka*.
The third [type] has six *nālikās* and is characterized by the *pīṭhamarda* and *vilāsavat* lovers;
the fourth should have ten *nālikās* and is the *aṅka* type, featuring playful gallants. *Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa* 6.305.
A *prakaraṇī* is indeed a type of *nāṭikā*, wherein the hero is a merchant-leader (*sārthavāha*) or the like, and the heroine is born of the same lineage as the hero. (VisSd 6.306)
The *hallīśa* has a single act and seven, eight, or ten female roles;

it features a single male character with elevated speech, is radiant with the *kaiśikī* style, possesses the *mukha* and *nirvahaṇa* junctures, and is established in many *tāla*s and *laya*s. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.307)

The *bhāṇikā* is characterized by smooth costumes, possesses both an opening (*mukha*) and a conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*), is composed in a single act (*aikāṅka*), and employs the *kaiśikī* and *bhāratī* styles of dramatic delivery. (VisSd 6.308)
The seven subsidiary elements here are the noble heroine, the dull-witted hero, introduction, arrangement, contradiction, and likewise apprehension. (Viśvavidyā 6.309)
Dedication, cessation, and withdrawal constitute the seventh; introduction is the mention of a matter by way of a relevant context. (VisSd 6.310)
The mastery of words expressing world-weariness is known as *vinyāsa*;
the destruction of delusion is *vibodha*, while false proclamation is *sādhvasa*. (VisSd 6.311)
Speech accompanied by apprehension, the surrendering of oneself through the affliction of anger, and the presentation of an illustrative example—this is called "cessation" (nivṛtti). VisSd 6.312.
They call "saṃhāra" (conclusion) the completion of a work;
it consists merely of what is to be heard, and it is of two kinds: composed in verse and in prose.
Verses composed with fixed meters are called *padya*; those not so constrained are *muktaka*.
A pair of such verses is a *yugmaka*, while three are intended to be a *sāndānitaka*.
A *kalāpaka* is considered to consist of four [verses], and a *kulaka* of five;
a *mahākāvya* is a composition in cantos (*sarga-bandha*), wherein the sole protagonist is a deity.
Whether they be Kṣatriyas of noble lineage endowed with the qualities of a *dhīrodātta* hero, or kings born of a single line, or even many of high birth; (VisSd 6.316)

Among the erotic, heroic, and peaceful sentiments, one is intended to be the primary sentiment (aṅgin), while all other sentiments serve as its subordinates (aṅga); likewise, all dramatic junctures (saṃdhis) are employed. (Viśvavidyā 6.317)
Whether the subject matter be an event derived from history or something else based on the conduct of virtuous people,
it should consist of four sections, and there should be a single fruit resulting from them.
At the beginning, there may be a salutation, a benediction, or simply the statement of the subject matter;
in some cases, there is the censure of the wicked and the like, as well as the praise of the virtues of the virtuous. (Viśvavidyā 6.319)
In this work, there are more than eight cantos, composed of verses in a single meter with other meters appearing at the conclusion, neither too short nor too long.
In some instances, a creation consisting of various meters is observed;
at the end of a creation, there may be an indication of the narrative of a future creation. (VisSd 6.321)
Twilight, the sun, the moon, night, the onset of darkness, day;
morning, midday, the hunt, mountains, seasons, forests, and the ocean. VisSd 6.322.
Union and separation, sages, heavens, cities, and sacrifices;
battles, departures, marriages, mantras, and the birth of sons, and so forth.

These [elements], along with their primary and secondary components, should be described here as appropriate, either by the name of the poet or the work, or by that of the hero or another character. (Viśvadha 6.324)
Its name is indeed "Sarga" (Creation) due to its narration of the subject matter of creation;
however, in this work of the Ṛṣis, there are further sections called "Ākhyānas" (Narratives).
In that work composed in the Prākṛta language, the sections are known as *āśvāsas*; it is written in the *skandhaka* meter, and in some places also in *galitakas*.
In this work composed in Apabhraṃśa, the cantos are designated as *kuḍavakas*,
and there are likewise various meters suitable for the Apabhraṃśa language.
Due to the rules of language and its specific grammatical elaborations, a *kāvya* is devoid of formal cantos (*sarga*);
it consists of verses directed toward a single theme and is free from the requirements of complete metrical junctions (*sandhi*). (VisSd 6.328)
A *khaṇḍakāvya* (fragmentary poem) follows a single portion of a [larger] poetic work;
whereas a *kośa* (anthology) is a collection of verses that are independent of one another. (VisSd 6.329)
That very same [composition], arranged according to the sequence of journeys, is exceedingly beautiful;
it consists of prose devoid of metrical scent (*vṛtta-gandha*) as well as prose that possesses the scent of meter (*muktaka* and *vṛtta-gandhin*).
There are four types of *cūrṇaka*, primarily consisting of *utkalikā*:
the first is devoid of compounds, while the latter is joined with metrical feet (*vṛtta*). (VisSd 6.331)

In a *kathā*, the subject matter is composed entirely in prose; it may be rich in long compounds in one part and characterized by few compounds in another, while being full of aesthetic flavor. (VisSd 6.332)
In some places here there may be an Āryā, and in others a Vaktra or Apavaktra;
at the beginning, there is a salutation in verse and a description of the meter of the wicked ones and so forth.
An *ākhyāyikā* should be like a *kathā*, with a recitation of the poet’s lineage;
in it, there may also be accounts of other poets, and here and there, verses (*padya*). (VisSd 6.334)
The division of narrative sections is called an *āśvāsa* (chapter);
it is composed in any meter whatsoever, such as *āryā*, *vaktra*, or *apavaktra*. (VisSd 6.335)
A poem composed of both prose and verse, which provides a hint of future events at the beginning under the guise of another subject, is called a *campū*. (VisSd 6.336)
A panegyric of a king composed in both prose and verse is called a *viruda*; however, a *karambhaka* is composed in various languages. (VisSd 6.337)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Dramatic and Poetic Works," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa. (7)
The Seventh Chapter: Determination of Defects.
Defects are those factors which detract from the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); they are further considered to be of five kinds.
Since these [qualities] occur in a word, in its constituent part, in a sentence, in its meaning, and even in aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Harshness, the three kinds of vulgarity, impropriety of meaning, and lack of usage; vulgarity, unintelligibility, ambiguity, indirect meaning, and obscurity. VisSd 7.2.
Inexpressiveness, obscenity, contradiction, excessive prolixity, and the state of having an undiscerned predicate-part belong to words and sentences. (VisSd 7.3)
Certain defects occur in these [words], both in parts of words and in whole words; namely, meaninglessness, lack of semantic competency, and likewise corruption of grammatical formation. (VisSd 7.4)
Adversity regarding the phonemes, the elision or corruption of the visarga, the presence of redundant or missing words, and the corruption of the meter; VisSd 7.5.
In the case of a *sandhi* (euphonic junction), there may be loss of excellence, harshness due to disjunction, indecorousness, or difficulty;
as well as the occurrence of a single word across two halves of a verse, and the resumption of a concluded [subject]. (VisSd 7.6)

The absence of the intended connection, the violation of the sequence, the lack of purpose for another, the non-expression of the expressed meaning, and likewise the breaking of the established sequence; VisSd_7.7 //
Omission, misplaced placement, the improper use of words or compounds, obscurity, and redundancy—these are defects that pertain solely to the sentence. (VisSd 7.8)
Lack of nourishment, faulty progression, vulgarity, contradiction, obscenity, and difficulty;
lack of freshness, lack of reason, explicitness, and contradiction. (VisSd 7.9)
Ambiguity, tautology, contradiction with renown or knowledge, expectancy, deviation from concomitance, and misplaced application; (Viśuddhimagga 7.10)

There is specification where there is no distinction, and likewise restriction where there is no restriction; furthermore, the reversal of these two occurs through the application of injunction and restatement. (VisSd 7.11)

The state of being free from tautology is proclaimed as a great merit; however, the expression of rasa by its own name, as well as that of the stable (sthāyin) and transitory (sañcārin) emotions, is a fault. (VisSd 7.12)
The manifestation [of rasa] is achieved with difficulty through the [proper presentation of] the consequents (*anubhāva*) and determinants (*vibhāva*);
likewise, there should be no untimely expansion or interruption, nor should there be repeated intensification. (VisSd 7.13)

The following line from the *Viśuddhimārga* is missing here: "The inclusion of impediments such as the non-essential [factors] of the non-essential [meditation]; the failure to connect with the essential [factor], and the mention of that which is not an essential factor.
"The failure to connect with the essential [factor], and the mention of that which is not an essential factor."
Excessive expansion of a member and the inversion of the primary elements.

Inappropriateness of meaning and other such defects are considered to reside in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); there is no possibility of defects belonging to figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) apart from these. (VisSd 7.15)
When the speaker is filled with anger, when the subject matter is highly provocative,
or when the sentiment (rasa) is the Furious (raudra) and so forth, extreme harshness of sound becomes a poetic quality.

Furthermore, vulgarity at the beginning of a love letter, a social gathering, and so forth, as well as the faults of "obscured meaning" (*nihatārtha*) and "unconventional usage" (*aprayukta*), may both be considered non-faults when they occur within a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) or similar figures.
The quality [of *apratītatva*] would consist in the speaker and the subject matter being unknown, or in the speaker himself reflecting [upon it], or in the word being stated again. (VisSd 7.18)
When that which has been prescribed is restated, or in cases of despondency, wonder, anger, dejection, as well as in *lāṭānuprāsa*, compassion, and conciliation; (7.19)
In the case of the suggested sense being transferred to another meaning (arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya), there is either emphasis on joy or certainty;
likewise, if it culminates in apparent censure (vyājastuti) or in doubt.

When the foremost of grammarians is the subject to be explained or the speaker, there is "difficulty" (kaṣṭatva) or "unpleasantness to hear" (duḥśravatva); whereas "vulgarity" (grāmyatva) occurs in the speech of the low-born.
But when a meaning is already well-known, the state of being causeless does not at all become a fault;
rather, in the convention of poets, the contradiction of what is well-known is considered a merit. (VisSd 7.22)

Dirtiness is described in relation to the sky and sin, while whiteness is attributed to laughter and fame; redness belongs to anger and passion, as do the lotuses and blue water-lilies found in rivers and oceans.
A flock of birds, such as swans and others, spreads across every reservoir of water; the moonlight is dear to the *cakra* birds, and during the rainy season, the swans depart for Lake Mānasa.

The *aśoka* tree blossoms from the stroke of a foot; the *bakula* blooms with the breaths of women; necklaces break upon the limbs of youths, and their hearts burst from the torments of separation. Just as the heart of a young man might be pierced by the arrows of the Flower-Bannered God—his bowstring being a garland of bees and his arrows made of flowers—it is likewise pierced by the side-glance of a woman. The day-lotus (*ambhoja*) blooms by day, while the night-lily (*kumuda*) blooms at night; the moonlight shines during the bright fortnight, and peacocks dance amidst the rumbling of clouds. Yet, no fruit ever appears upon the *aśoka*.

There would be no jasmine in spring, nor flowers and fruits from trees that possess the essence of fragrance; other such matters occurring in the conventions of poets should be inferred from the compositions of great poets. VisSd 7.25.
In words such as "bow" and "bowstring," the words "bow" and so forth must be employed to convey the sense of being "mounted" and so on; these [words] remain [in use]. (VisSd 7.26)
In cases such as "immersed in bliss" (ānandamagna) and so forth, when uttered [in a specific context], the deficiency of words is a merit;
in some instances it is neither a fault nor a merit, while in others an extra word is a merit. (VisSd 7.27)
The resumption of what has already been concluded is neither a fault nor a merit in any case;
in some instances, "pregnant" expression (garbhitatva) is a merit, as is the falling away of excellence (patat-prakarṣatā). (VisSd 7.28)

In some cases, there is no fault in expressing a transitory emotion by its own name, provided that its representation through the ensuants (*anubhāva*) and the determinants (*vibhāva*) is not appropriate. (VisSd 7.29)
The statement of a contradictory element, such as a transition (*sañcārī*), is a poetic merit when it is sublated;
likewise, it is so when there is a recollection of the contradictory or when they are stated with equality. *Viśvavidyā-sādhana* 7.30.
There would be no mutual contradiction between two things that have attained the status of being both the primary and the subordinate;
and in the case of imitation, there is no faultfulness whatsoever in any of the defects.

By wise men, through the principle of appropriateness (*aucitya*), the absence of fault, the presence of excellence, and the state of being neither in other defects should also be understood. (VisSd 7.32)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, "The Exposition of Defects," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
(8) The Eighth Chapter.
The determination of the qualities (guṇas):
when rasa is the predominant element, its qualities are like the attributes of valor and so forth possessed by one who has attained it.
These qualities—sweetness (mādhurya), vigor (ojas), and clarity (prasāda)—are threefold. (VisSd 8.1)
Sweetness is said to consist of a joy arising from the melting of the mind;
it is present in increasing measure, respectively, in the *saṃbhoga*, the compassionate, the *vipralambha*, and the peaceful [rasas].
On the head [of the vowel] are the groups of consonants joined with the letter *a*, excluding *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *da*, and *ḍha*;
for the manifestation of that [vowel], the letters *ra* and *ṇa* and the short vowels have become the causes. (VisSd 8.3)
Absence of repetition or only slight repetition, as well as sweet composition—this is called *ojas*, which is the expansion of the mind and its state of brilliance. (VisSd 8.4)
However, this class [of consonants] reaches its maximum intensity in the heroic (vīra), the loathsome (bībhatsa), and the furious (raudra) rasas respectively;
when joined with the first and third [sibilants], the letters at the end of that class [become even more intense].

Above or below, or in both positions, the letters with the *repha* (ṛ), together with *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha*, as well as the letters *śa* and *ṣa*, have become the manifestors of that [sound]. (VisSd 8.6)
Likewise, [there is] that which abounds in compounds, possesses a sense of dramatic intensity and boldness,
and furthermore, those qualities known as *śleṣa* (paronomasia), *samādhi* (concentration), *audārya* (magnificence), and *prasāda* (clarity).
The qualities mentioned by the ancients are included within *ojas*;
*kānti* and *sukumāratā* result from the abandonment of vulgarity and harshness of sound. (VisSd 8.8)
In some cases, however, a fault is actually a form of equanimity whose nature is non-distinction from the path;
otherwise, its inclusion among the aforementioned qualities occurs accordingly.
Vigor, clarity, sweetness, delicacy, and loftiness—these subordinate qualities are accepted as such because their absence constitutes a defect. (VisSd 8.10)

The clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*) arises through the figure of speech *svabhāvokti* (description of intrinsic nature); furthermore, it constitutes the quality named *kānti* (loveliness) in relation to *rasadhvani* (suggestion of aesthetic flavor) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion). (VisSd 8.11)
Conciseness (*śleṣa*) is merely a form of variety and not a fault; it is subordinate to evenness (*samatā*).
Furthermore, because of this, concentration (*samādhi*) does not possess the status of a quality (*guṇa*); therefore, there are no separate qualities of meaning.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Qualities," in the Sāhityadarpaṇa.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The determination of *rīti*:
*Rīti* is the arrangement of words, like a particular configuration of limbs;
it serves to assist the *rasas* and other elements, and it is of four kinds. (VisSd 9.1)
Now, there are the Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī, and likewise the Lāṭikā styles; a composition characterized by grace is that which is fashioned with phonemes that manifest sweetness. (VisSd 9.2)
The Vaidarbha style is desired as being either without compounds or with few compounds;
whereas the *bandha* (composition) that employs letters manifesting *ojas* (vigour) is considered *āḍambara* (bombastic).

The Gauḍī style abounds in compounds; the other two [Vaidarbhī and Pāñcālī] are characterized by the remaining [simple] syllables. A composition consisting of five or six words joined together is considered Pāñcālikā.
The Lāṭī style, however, stands between the Vaidarbhī and Pāñcālī styles;
yet, in some cases, due to the propriety of the speaker and other factors, the arrangement and other elements may differ.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Styles" (*rīti-vivecana*), in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
[10] The Tenth Chapter.
The *alaṅkāras* (ornaments) are those unstable properties of word and meaning that produce an excellence of beauty;
they assist the *rasas* and so forth, like bracelets and other such [ornaments]. (VisSd 10.1)

[Verbal Ornamentations: That which appears as a repetition of meaning at first hearing, though it resides in words of different forms, is the semblance of tautology (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*). (VisSd 10.2)
Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is a similarity of sounds even when there is a difference in vowel;
it consists of the single repetition of a group of consonants in various ways. (VisSd 10.3)
The similarity of many [words] in a single way, or of one [word] in many ways, whether occurring repeatedly or even just once, is considered to be *vṛtty-anuprāsa*. (VisSd 10.4)
When there is a similarity of a consonant at a single place of articulation, such as the palate and so forth, because it is to be uttered [there], this is desired as *śruti-anuprāsa*.
If a consonant, remaining as it is, is repeated along with its accompanying vowel because it is to be joined with the final [word], that is indeed *antyānuprāsa* (final alliteration). VisSd 10.6.
The repetition of both word and meaning by way of intent alone is called *lāṭānuprāsa*;
thus, *anuprāsa* is considered to be of five kinds.
When there is a single meaning for a sequence of vowels and consonants that otherwise have distinct meanings,
its repetition in that very same order is called *yamaka*.
If one person should interpret a statement intended for one purpose in another way—
either through punning or through intonation— that is *vakrokti* (circuitous speech), and it is thus twofold.
When a sentence consists of words that are identical in form across various languages, this is accepted as the fallacy called "Identity of Language" (bhāṣāsama).

When multiple meanings are expressed through phonetically connected words, it is called *śleṣa* (paronomasia). This occurs through the connection of phonemes (*varṇa*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), genders (*liṅga*), verbal roots (*prakṛti*), or even entire words (*pada*). (Viśvavidyā-sadana 10.11)
Due to the combination of grammatical case, number, and language, it is eightfold;
furthermore, it is threefold as being with word-break (*sabhaṅga*), without word-break (*abhaṅga*), and consisting of both.
When syllables serve as the cause for the form of verses and so forth, it is called *citram* (puzzle-poetry);
however, because it acts as an obstacle to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the *prahelikā* (riddle) is not considered an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

That [figure] consists merely in the variety of expression, such as the transposition or addition of syllables; whereas Simile (upamā) occurs when there is similarity between two things in a single sentence, provided there is no difference in their essential nature. VisSd 10.14.

If it possesses the common attribute (sāmānyadharma), a word expressing comparison (aupamyavācin), the standard of comparison (upamāna), and the object of comparison (upameya) explicitly stated, then this [simile] is complete. However, this [type of simile] is as follows: || ViśSd 10.15 ||
The *śrauti* [upamā] occurs when the words *yathā*, *iva*, *vā*, or the suffix *vat*—which has the sense of *iva*—is present;
the *ārthī* occurs where words such as *tulya* or *samāna* are used, or where the suffix *vat* has the sense of "equal to. (VisSd 10.16)
In a derivative (taddhita), in a compound (samāsa), or even in a sentence, that [simile] is complete with all six elements;
it is "elliptical" (luptā) if one or two of the common attributes (sāmānyadharma) and so forth are omitted. (VisSd 10.17)

Or, when there is no mention of the three [factors], that [metaphor] may be based on the literal sense (śrauti) or the implied sense (ārthī), as before. When there is an elision of the *dharma*, it is like the "full" (pūrṇā) type; however, that [elision of the *dharma*] occurs without the literal sense in the case of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).
In the two types [of compounds] prescribed for the locative case and the object of the action, as well as in *kyac* and *kyaṅ*,
and in *ṇamul* where the object and the agent are coreferential— thus, it occurs again in five ways.
When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not employed, there are two types [of ellipsis]: in the sentence (*vākya*) and in the compound (*samāsa*).
When the word expressing the comparison (*aupamyavācin*) is elided, there are two types in the compound: in the *samāsa* and in the *kvip* suffix.

In a compound or in a sentence, it is twofold when there is the elision of the attribute (*dharma*) and the object of comparison (*upamāna*); when the attribute, the particle *iva*, and so forth are elided, it is twofold as occurring within a *kvip*-derivative or a compound.

When the object of comparison (*upameya*) is elided, it occurs in a single suffix (*pratyaya*), namely *kyac*; when both the quality (*dharma*) and the object of comparison are elided, it is another [type]; and when all three are elided, it resides in a compound (*samāsa*). (VisSd 10.22)
Thus, there may be twenty-seven varieties of simile;
in some cases the common quality (*guṇa*) is of a single form, while in others it is differentiated. 10.23.

When there is a distinction between the original object and its reflection, or when the difference exists merely in words, this is a *vācyopamā* (expressed simile) occurring in a single locus. || 10.24 ||

Where the simile of taste (*rasanopamā*) is said to exist through equality, it occurs when the object of comparison (*upameya*) becomes the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in the subsequent [clause]. (VisSd 10.25)

A string simile (*mālopamā*) occurs when many points of comparison are seen for a single [subject]; whereas *ananvaya* (non-connection) is the state of being both the object of comparison and the point of comparison for that very same thing.
This is considered *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) when two things are compared by way of alternation;
*smaraṇa* (remembrance) is said to be the recollection of an object resulting from the experience of something similar. (VisSd 10.27)
Metaphor (*rūpaka*) consists in the superimposition of the nature of one thing upon another object that is not denied;
it is of three kinds: *paraṃparita* (transferred), *sāṅga* (with parts), and *niraṅga* (without parts). VisSd 10.28.
Where the superimposition of one thing is the cause for the superimposition of another,
they call that *paraṃparita* (successive metaphor), based on either a pun (*śliṣṭa*) or a non-pun (*aśliṣṭa*).
There are four types [of metaphor]: the individual, the exclusive, the garland-like, and the "with-limbs" (sāṅga).
If there is a representation of the whole together with its parts, that is indeed "with-limbs. (VisSd 10.30)
The first [type] has all things as its object and manifests in a single location; this is the view when all the objects of superimposition are expressed by words. (VisSd 10.31)
Where the status of being the object belongs to something [else], that is *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest).
That too is twofold: the *niraṅga* (limbless), which is the metaphorical representation of the whole alone. (VisSd 10.32)
Because it consists solely of a series [of metaphors], there are eight varieties of metaphor (rūpaka) by that means;
sometimes the objects to be superimposed are seen as being punned even within a combined metaphor (saṅgarūpaka). VisSd 10.33.

That very same metaphor (rūpaka) which possesses the distinction of being superimposed [upon the subject] is such when the object of superimposition serves as the sense-object for the primary meaning and is thus useful for the contextual theme. (VisSd 10.34)
Metaphorical identification (pariṇāma) is of two kinds: that which has a common substratum and that which does not.
Doubt consists of uncertainty regarding the subject at hand or another object, arising from a flash of intuition (pratibhā). 10.35.
It is threefold: pure, that which has certainty within it, and that which ends in certainty.
Thus, the cognition of something as what it is not, arising from a flash of intuition due to similarity, is the state of delusion.
When there is a single [object] appearing in multiple ways—either due to some difference among the perceivers or likewise among the objects—that is called *ullekha* (poetic delineation). 10.37.
Apahnuti (concealment) consists in establishing something else after negating the subject under discussion, having somehow indicated some meaning that is intended to be concealed. (VisSd 10.38)
If she [the speaker] should alter it otherwise, either through a pun (*śleṣa*) or in another way, that too is *apahnuti* (concealment).
Furthermore, *niścaya* (ascertainment) is the re-establishment of the subject at hand after having negated something else.
The poetic fancy (saṃbhāvanotprekṣā) consists in conceiving the subject at hand as having the nature of another;
it is considered to be first of two kinds: the expressed (vācyā) and the implied (pratīyamānā).
When the object of comparison (*vācya*) is employed, there is *utprekṣā* with a verbal suffix (*vādi*); when it is not employed, it is the other type (*parā*).
Furthermore, that which is to be imagined—whether it be a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a substance (*dravya*)—belongs to both types.
Each of those eight [types of conceptualization] is further divided into two— based on the conceit of existence and non-existence—
and again, because the cause consists of qualities, actions, and essential natures.
Furthermore, in that context, the designations of the objects of expression become thirty-two-fold;
excluding substance, all [the remaining categories] are threefold, pertaining to essential nature, fruit, and cause.

In that regard, the causes for stating or not stating [the reason] are twofold; they reside in the essential nature [of the reason], are perceived as distinct [types], and each resides in both the result and the cause. (VisSd 10.44)
Each of those [two types] is further divided into two, according to whether the subject at hand is explicitly stated or left unstated;
that which arises from another poetic figure (alaṅkāra) possesses an even greater degree of aesthetic charm.
When the determination [of identity] is established, it is called *atiśayokti* (hyperbole):
non-difference despite difference, and non-connection despite connection, as well as their reversals. (Viśvadatta 10.46)

That [inference] consisting of priority and posteriority is considered to be fivefold, whether it occurs between the effect and the cause, or between the subject matter at hand and other things. (VisSd 10.47)
If there were a connection with a single attribute, that would be *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing);
however, when there is a connection between the irrelevant and the relevant, it is called *dīpaka* (illumination).
Now, if a single agent were to be involved in multiple actions,
that would be *prativastūpamā*, provided there is an implied similarity between two sentences.
Even when a single common property is indicated separately,
an example (dṛṣṭānta) serves as a reflection of an entity that possesses that same property.
Whether the connection between things is possible or impossible in some cases, that [figure] by which the state of being an original and its reflection is made known is *nidarśanā*. (VisSd 10.51)
The figure of speech called *vyatireka* (distinction) consists of the superiority of the object compared (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or conversely, its inferiority;
it is of one kind when the cause [of this difference] is stated, and of three kinds when the cause is unstated. (VisSd 10.52)
Since even the fourfold [simile] is understood through word, meaning, and implication, it becomes twelvefold; thus, including *śleṣa*, there are twenty-four types.
Each [type] would again be of forty-eight kinds when combined;
furthermore, there is one [kind] where, by the force of the meaning, a single [word] is expressive of two [meanings]. (VisSd 10.54)
That is Sahokti (Simultaneous Description) when it is based upon a fundamental Hyperbole (Atiśayokti);
Vinokti (Description by Absence) occurs when, without another thing, something else is neither good nor bad. (VisSd 10.55)

*Samāsokti* (Abridged Expression) occurs where, through actions, signs, or adjectives that are similar, there is a superimposition of the conventional behavior of another thing upon the subject at hand. (VisSd 10.56)
The *parikara* (embellishment) is considered to consist of the aforementioned qualifiers used with intentional meaning;
*śleṣa* (paronomasia) is the expression of multiple meanings by words that, by their very nature, possess a single meaning. (VisSd 10.57)
In some cases, the particular is [inferred] from the general, or the general from the particular;
the cause from the effect, or the effect from the cause; and likewise, the equal from the equal.

If the subject at hand is understood from that which is not the subject at hand, then there are five ways in which Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Praise) occurs; furthermore, Vyājastuti (Dissembling Praise) is also mentioned.
When praise and censure are to be understood through words that express blame and praise respectively,
it is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) when that which is actually implied is stated by means of a figurative turn of phrase.
If the universal is established by the particular, or the particular by that [universal], and if this effect is established by the cause, and the cause by the effect; 10.61.
From that [Arthāntaranyāsa], there are eight types based on similarity and its opposite;
when the reason is expressed as the meaning of a word within a sentence, it is called Kāvyaliṅga.
Inference, however, is knowledge characterized by a distinct form, arising from the proof of that which is to be proven;
it is the cause for the expression [of the probandum] as non-different from the reason, together with that which possesses the reason.
If that which is favorable is made unfavorable, yet rendered favorable again, for the purpose of expressing a specific quality of the intended object, [it is called "the contrary"]. (VisSd 10.64)
Paralipsis (ākṣepa) is a semblance of negation; it is twofold, according to whether it refers to what is yet to be said or what has already been said.
The other [type] is considered a semblance of an injunction regarding an undesirable matter. (VisSd 10.65)
When it is said that the production of an effect occurs without a cause, that is proclaimed to be of two kinds, according to whether its motive has been stated or unstated. (VisSd 10.66)
When the cause exists but the effect is absent, there is likewise the figure of speech called *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation), which is of two kinds.
*Jāti* (birth) [is expressed] by four [factors] beginning with birth; *guṇa* (quality) [is expressed] by three [factors] beginning with quality. (10.67)
When action appears as if mutually contradictory with another action or a substance, or when a substance appears as if contradictory with another substance, that contradiction is of ten forms.
Inconsistency (*asaṅgati*) occurs when cause and effect occupy different locations;
it also occurs when two qualities or two actions belonging to the cause and the effect are mutually contradictory. (VisSd 10.69)
When that which has been undertaken is fruitless and results in misfortune, or when there is a union of two discordant things—that is considered the "uneven" (viṣama). VisSd 10.70.
Praise that is appropriate to a worthy object should be equal to its nature;
it is "variegated" when the performance of something seemingly contradictory leads to the attainment of a desired result. (VisSd 10.71)
When there is an excess of either the support or the supported, it is called "excessive.
Both are mutually the cause of each other's single activity; thus they are reciprocal.
That which is to be deposited is without a substratum, both one and yet the object of many;
it is something produced by one who is either incapable or otherwise [capable] of performing the effect.
The accomplishment of an effect through destiny is thus a threefold excellence;
however, *vyāghāta* (contradiction) occurs when something is done by someone in a certain way. (VisSd 10.74)
If another person performs that same task by a different means, or if it is performed in a contrary way despite the ease with which the task could have been accomplished; ||| VisSd_10.75 |||
If each preceding element serves as the cause for each subsequent one, then it would be a "garland of causes" (kāraṇamālā); however, that [specific type] is the "lamp-garland" (mālādīpaka).
If, subsequently, [the reason] is connected to the subjects by means of a single property, such that each preceding [property] serves as a qualifier for each succeeding one; 10.77.
If it is established or excluded, then there would be two kinds of single series;
the excellence of an object in successive stages is called its essence.
The non-enumeration (anuddeśa) of those things already enumerated is according to their respective order;
