in some cases, one [is placed] in many, and one is placed individually in each in sequence. (Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi 10.79)
If it exists or is performed, then it is accepted as a synonym;
exchange (parivṛtti) or barter (vinimaya) occurs through [objects] that are equal, inferior, or superior. (VisSd 10.80)
Whether from a question or even from what is not a question,
if there arises an exclusion of others (anyāpoha) regarding the object stated, then that [exclusion] is either verbal or objective.

If an inference follows from an answer to a question that is a *parisaṃkhyā* (an exclusive specification), or if there is an answer despite the absence of a question, even though it is improbable to occur repeatedly; [then it is a *praśnottara*]. (VisSd 10.82)
The apprehension of another meaning by way of the "stick-and-cake" principle (*daṇḍāpūpikā*) is accepted as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);
and contradiction between two [alternatives] of equal strength constitutes doubt (*vikalpa*), because of the intervention [of uncertainty]. (VisSd 10.83)

This is a case of conjunction (*samuccaya*): when there is already one means for accomplishing an effect, if one who possesses that [other] means also applies himself to it, according to the maxim of the *khalekapotika* (the simultaneous falling of pigeons upon a threshing floor). VisSd 10.84.
Two qualities or two actions may occur simultaneously, or a quality and an action [may occur together];
this is *samādhi* when a task that is difficult becomes easy due to fate or the advent of another circumstance.
If one who is unable to retaliate against an enemy resorts to contempt for that enemy's possessions, it serves to establish the enemy's own excellence. (VisSd 10.86)
The conceptualization of a well-known object of comparison as the subject of comparison, or the statement of its fruitlessness, is called *pratīpa* (the inverse). (VisSd 10.87)

Having stated the extreme excellence of an exceedingly superior object, some have declared *pratīpa* (the inverse) even when that [superior object] is employed as a standard of comparison. (VisSd 10.88)
*Mīlita* (the concealed) is the hiding of an object by something possessing similar characteristics.
*Sāmānya* (the common) is the identification of the subject with another due to its qualities being similar to those of others. (VisSd 10.89)
One who possesses those qualities [of the object] abandons their own qualities to grasp the exceedingly superior qualities [of that object];
however, one who does not take on its form is "one without those qualities," even though the cause for it exists.
When a subtle meaning, though perceived, is indicated by some particular artifice through outward appearance or gesture, that is called the "subtle" [type of indication]. (VisSd 10.91)
*Vyājokti* (disguised expression) is the concealment of a matter that has become manifest through some pretext;
*svabhāvokti* (description of nature) is the depiction of the action, form, or character of something whose meaning is difficult to grasp. *Viśeṣastava* 10.92.
That which consists in the appearance of a present perception of a marvelous object—whether it has already occurred or is yet to occur—is called *bhāvika*. (VisSd 10.93)
The excellence that transcends the world is called the "noble" (udātta) in a subject; or it may be the conduct of great beings that serves as an auxiliary to the matter at hand. (VisSd 10.94)

When the sentiments (rasas), the transitory states (bhāvas), their semblances (tad-ābhāsas), as well as the subsidence of a state (bhāva-praśama) and the state of being subordinate (guṇī-bhūtatva), attain [the status of the primary meaning], then they become poetic ornaments (alaṅkṛtis). 10.95.
The *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita* [styles] are, respectively, so named when there is the arousal of a *bhāva*, its combination, and its mixture. (Viśadālaṃkāra 10.96)
If these very same figures of speech are mutually intermingled, then there are two distinct figures: *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) and likewise *saṅkara* (blending). *VisSd_10.97*

Furthermore, *saṅkara* (commixture) occurs in three ways: when figures of speech stand in the relation of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitva*), when they reside in a single substratum (*ekāśrayasthiti*), and when there is doubt (*sandigdhatva*). (10.98)

Having examined this *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, a treatise composed by the illustrious Viśvanātha Kavirāja—the son of the great poet Candra and grandson of the illustrious Candraśekhara—let the wise easily understand the entirety of the principles of literary aesthetics. (VisSd 10.99)

As long as she whose face resembles the bright moon adorns the lap of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, so long may this composition, which delights the minds of poets, remain celebrated in the world. (VisSd 10.100)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Sāhityadarpaṇa, composed by the sovereign of rhetoricians, the Great Chamberlain and Minister of Foreign Affairs, the illustrious Viśvanātha Kavirāja.
